column4: Directive laying down a procedure for the provision of information in the field of technical standards and regulations
column16:
The Directive directly regulates Member States and national standards institutions by requiring them to notify the Commission, other Member States, and designated standards bodies of draft standards, standards programmes, and draft technical regulations before their adoption.

The Commission is the central coordinating authority. It receives notifications of draft standards and technical regulations, circulates them to Member States, may issue comments, may trigger standstill periods, may indicate its intention to propose Community legislation, and oversees the operation of the notification procedure.

National standards institutions are regulated participants in the regime. They must notify standards programmes and draft standards, cooperate with other standards institutions, and refrain from developing conflicting national standards when a European standard is being prepared. European standards organisations, particularly CEN and CENELEC, participate in the regime through the development of European standards when requested.

column4: Decision on the promotion of standardization in Europe and the preparation and implementation of standards in the field of information technology and telecommunications
column16:
The Commission is the central coordinating authority. It identifies standardisation priorities, prepares work programmes, commissions technical work, mandates European standards organisations and specialised technical bodies to develop standards and functional specifications, monitors implementation, and reports on progress.

Member States are regulated participants in the regime. They must promote the use of European and international standards in public procurement, refer to those standards when drafting technical regulations where appropriate, and participate in the implementation of the Decision through the relevant committees.
Specifically, contracting authorities and telecommunications administrations are also subject to the regime, as they are expected to use the relevant standards and functional specifications in procurement and network-access arrangements.

Standard setting is then privatised to European standard organisations and specialised technical bodies in the information technology and telecommunications sector, particularly, CEN, CENELEC, and CEPT (the early version of ETSI). They develop European standards, pre-standards, functional specifications, testing specifications, and related technical documents under mandates/invitations issued by the Commission. They should, where appropriate, rely on international standards and technincal specification in the telecommunications.

The Committee titled "Senior Officials Group on standardization in the field of Information Technology" consults the Commission.

column4: Resolution of 30 June 1988 (5) on the development of the common market for telecommunications services and equipment
column16:
Taken from Directive 98/13/EC: (5) Whereas the Council, in its resolution of 30 June 1988 (5) on the development of the common market for telecommunications services and equipment, has confirmed as a major goal in the telecommunications policy the full mutual recognition of type approval for terminal equipment on the basis of the rapid development of common European conformity specifications;

The Resolution defines several goals:
1. Establish an integrated and interoperable Community telecommunications network.
2. Create an open internal market for telecommunications services through Open Network Provision (ONP).
3. Promote Europe-wide telecommunications services with common pricing principles and operator cooperation.
4. Complete the internal market for telecommunications terminal equipment through mutual recognition and common specifications.
5. Ensure fair competition by separating regulatory and operational functions and opening procurement markets.
6. Promote common European telecommunications standards.
7. Strengthen European cooperation in telecommunications research and development.
8. Support the social transition to new telecommunications technologies through skills development, social dialogue, and data protection.
9. Improve telecommunications infrastructure in less-favoured regions to reduce regional disparities.
10. Develop a common Community approach to satellite communications.
11. Coordinate the Community's position in international telecommunications policy and negotiations.

column4: Commission Directive 88/301/EEC of 16 May 1988 on competition in the markets in telecommunications terminal equipment
column16:
The Commission Directive requires Member States to withdraw any special or exlusive rights granted to undertakings in relation to the importation, marketing, connection, bringing into service or maintenance of telecommunications terminal equipment, and to inform the Commission of the measures taken or draft legislation introduced to that end.

The Commission Directive also requires Member States to permit economic operators to import, market, connect, bring into service and maintain terminal equipment. Member States may nevertheless refuse to allow terminal equipment where it does not comply with the relevant technical specifications. They may also require economic operators to possess the technical qualifications needed to connect, bring into service and maintain terminal equipment, provided that the requirements are based on objective, nondiscriminatory and publicly available criteria.

The Directive also requires Member States to publish a list of all technical specifications and type-approval procedures applicable to terminal equipment.

The Member States must also ensure that from July 1989, the responsibility for drawing up the specifications referred to in Article 5, monitoring their application and granting type-approval is entrusted to a body independent of public or private undertakings offering goods and/or services in the telecommunications sector. 

This independent body exercises public regulatory, supervisory and approval functions and is therefore coded as a regulatory authority rather than a regulatory intermediary. In Case C-202/88, France v Commission, the Court of Justice upheld the validity of the relevant provisions of Directive 88/301/EEC. In Case C-69/91, Decoster, the Court confirmed that responsibility for technical specifications, monitoring and type approval must be separated from telecommunications undertakings. The Commission monitors Member State compliance with these requirements.

Member States must also take the necessary steps to ensure that undertakings within the meaning of Article 1 allow their customers to terminate, with maximum notice period of one year, leasing or maintenance contracts.

Member States must provide the Commission with an annual report containing the information necessary to monitor implementation of the Directive.

column4: Directive  on the establishment of the internal market for telecommunications services through the implementation of open network provision
column16:
The aim of this Directive is to harmonize the conditions for open and efficient access to and use of public telecommunications networks and, where applicable, public telecommunications services.

The Directive requires the Member States to inform the Commission on bodies to which they have granted special or exclusive rights. Special or exclusive rights means the rights granted by a Member State or a public authority to one or more public or private bodies through any legal, regulatory or administrative instrument reserving to them the right to provide a service or undertake an activity.
The Directive promotes open network conditions that meet key principles like objectivity, transparency, equality, and non-discrimination. Member States can restrict these based on essential needs such as security, network integrity, interoperability, and data protection. No further restrictions on public network use are allowed except those linked to special or exclusive rights granted by Member States and compatible with Community law. (in Commission Directives, the EU aims to withdraw the states from assigning such rights).

The Commission is tasked with drawing up a work program each year. In it, the Commission needs to initiate detailed analyses, invite public comments, and, where appropriate, request that the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) draw up European standards, harmonized technical interfaces and/or service features, and draw up proposals for open network provision conditions.

The Directive also relies on standards referenced in the OJEC, which carry a presumption of conformity regarding compliance with the relevant essential requirements and the requirements of open and efficient access.
Reference to European Standards may be made compulsory to the extent strictly necessary to ensure such interoperability and to improve freedom of choice for users.

column4: Commission Directive on competition in the markets for telecommunications services
column16:
The aim of this commission Directive is to progressively introducing competition into the telecommunications market. The programme does not concern mobile telephony and paging services, and mass communication services such as radio for television.

The Commission Directive requires Member States to withdraw all special or exclusive rights for the supply of telecommunications services other than voice telephony and to take the measures necessary to ensure that any operator is entitled to supply such telecommunications services.
Member States which make the supply of such services subject to a licensing or declaration procedure aimed at compliance with the essential requirements shall ensure that the conditions for the grant of licences are objective, non-discriminatory and transparent, that reasons are given for any refusal, and that there is a procedure for appealing against any such refusal.

Member States which maintain special or exclusive rights for the provision and operation of public telecommunications networks shall take the necessary measures to make the conditions governing access to the networks objective and non-discriminatory and publish them.

They must ensure that he control of type approval and mandatory specifications, the allocation of frequencies and surveillance of usage conditions are carried out by a body independent of the telecommunications organizations.

Member States shall ensure that as soon as the relevant special or exclusive rights have been withdrawn, telecommunications organizations make it possible for customers bound to them by a contract with more than one year to run for the supply of telecommunications services which was subject to such a right at the time it was concluded to terminate the contract at six months' notice.

Member States shall communicate to the Commission the necessary information to allow it to draw up, for a period of three years, at the end of each year, an overall report on the application of this Directive.
column17: This Directive operationalises self-regulation primarily by opening telecommunications services to market competition while allowing operators to organise and provide services within a framework of public rules. Once exclusive rights are removed (Article 2), operators are free to enter telecommunications markets, determine their commercial offerings, pricing, and service models, provided they comply with objective, transparent and non-discriminatory licensing conditions where these exist.

column4: Directive on the approximation of the laws of the Member States concerning telecommunications terminal equipment
column16:
The directive directly regulates manufacturers of equiptment which is capable of being connected to the public telecommunications network requiring them to accompany it with a manufacturer or supplier's declartion. Article 2 meanwhile regulates instances where the manufacturer sells equiptment that is capable to connect to the network, but it sells them for an entirely different purpose, for instance private use. 

According to Article 4, terminal equiptment must ensure user and employee's safety, electromagnetic compatability requirements, protecting the network from harm, effective use of the radio frequency spectrum, and its with public telecommunications network equipment for the purpose of establishing connection

Notified bodies support this declarations by receiving of the declaration when the product is placed on the market for the first time. The notified bodies can request to justify the equiptment's intended purpose, its function, and the market segments it is intended for. 

The directive assign core regulatory responsibilities to the member states to take all appropriate measures to ensure that terminal equiptment complies with the requirements set by the directive and that it may not be connected to the public telecommunications network. They must also take all appropriate measures to ensure that equiptment is disconnected from the public telecommunications network.
They must presume compliance when the equiptment confirm with national standards; member states publish the reference to national standards in the OJEC.
If the member states find that an equiptment does not comply with the essential requirements when properly used in accordance with the purpose intended by the manufacturer, it shall take all approprirate measures to withdraw it from the market, and inform the Commission of its decision and whether it is due to incorrect application of the harmonised standards or common technical regulations or shortcomings of these standards and regulations. It should also take appropriate measures against whoever affixed a CE mark.

Member states also designate notified bodies for carrying out the certification, product checks, and associated surveillance tasks pertaining to the conformity assessment procedures. Annex V sets the minimum criteria for designating a notified body. They may also designate test laboratories to carry out tests relating to the conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies applying a criteria specified in relevant harmonised standards for designating such laboratories. The Commission publishes the lists for notified bodies and test laboratories.

The Commission's task is to adopt common technical regulations. Both it and the member states can bring a standard in fron of the relevant committee where they find it exceed or do not entirely meet the essential requirements.
The Commission may also enter into consultation with relevant parties when an equiptment is withdrawned due to incorrect application of shortcommings of standards and techincal regulations. It will bring the issue in front of the relevant commitee, called the Approvals Committee for Terminal Equipment (ACTE)
column17:
Self-regulation is operationalised through process-based regulation enhanced by notified bodies and test laboratories.
The responsibility lies in the hand of manufacturers who can choose between EC type-examination and declaration based on one of two procedures (annexes I-III) or EC declaration of conformity (Annex IV).

Notified bodies issue EC type-examination certification based on Annex I and the procedures defined in Annexes II or III, or a decision of quality assurance assessment as referred to in Annex IV, and also issue an administrative approval for the connection of the concerned terminal equipment to the public telecommunications network. Notified bodies must inform other notified bodies of the relevant information concerning the quality system or certificates issued and withdrawn. 
Annex V requires notified bodies to be independent, technically competent, adequately resourced, impartial, insured against liability, and bound by professional secrecy

CE marks carry the identifying symbol of the notified body, and the notified body will withdraw if it is established that the equiptment does not fonform to an approve type, or does not meet the essential requirements per the approved type, or fails to fulfil his obligations.

Annex I - EC TYPE-EXAMINATION (followed by procedures  described in annex II or III): the notified body ascertains and attests that an equiptment meets the provisions. Documentation shall enable the conformity of the product with the essential requirements, with the notified body examining the documentation, verify conformity, perform the appropriate examinations and necessary tests against the requirements and technical regulations, and issue EC type-examination certificate. The applicant must inform the notified body of any modification which must receive additional approval.

Annex II - CONFORMITY TO TYPE: The manufacturer or his representative ensures and declares that the product confirm with the type described in the EC type-examination certification and satisfy the requirements of the Directive. The manufacturer must take all measures to ensure that the manufacturing process assures compliance and keep a copy of the declaration of conformity for 10 years. A notified bofy chosen by the manufacturer must carry out product checks at random intervals and sample products to examine and test whether the product confirm with the requirements set by the directive. 

Annex III - PRODUCTION QUALITY ASSURANCE: the manufacturer ensures and declares the product confirm with the type described in the EC type-examination certificate. It then operate an approved quality system for production, final inspection and testing, and is subjected to monitoring. The manufacturer lodge an application for assessesm of his quality system with a notified body of his concern and include all relevant information and documentation. The quality system must ensure compliance. The notified body then assess the quality system to determine whether it satisfies the requirements, and assume conformity if the quality system aligns with a relevant harmonised standard. It will do inspection visit of the premises, particularly the location of manufacture, inspecting, and testing, and storage. The notified body will also carry out audits at reasonable intervals to make sure the quality systems are applied and maintained. It is permitted to do unexpected visits.

Annex IV - full quality assurance: Annex IV establishes a full quality-assurance procedure. Manufacturers remain responsible for conformity and must operate a documented quality system covering design, manufacture, inspection, and testing. A notified body assesses and approves the quality system, evaluates any subsequent modifications, and conducts periodic and unannounced surveillance audits to ensure continued compliance. Notified bodies also inform one another of quality-system approvals and withdrawals.
The notified body shall assess in particular whether the quality control system ensures conformity of the products with the requirements of the Directive in the light of the relevant documentation supplied. The auditing team shall have at least one member experienced as an assessor in the product technology concerned. 
The manufacturer or his authorized representative shall keep the notified body that has approved the quality system informed of any intended updating of the quality system. The notified body shall evaluate the modifications proposed and decide whether the amended quality system will still satisfy the requirements referred to in point 3.2. or whether a re-assessment is required.

The notified body will also carry out surveillance activities as described in the annex to make sure that the manufacturer duly fulfils the obligations arising out of the approved quality system. The notified body should carry the audits at reasonable intevals yet may pay unexpceted visits. It will inform other notified bodies regarding qaulity systems approval or withdrawal.

column4: Directive on the application of open network provision to leased lines
column16:
The directive aims to harmonize the conditions for open and efficient access to and use of the leased lines provided to users on public telecommunications networks. The Directive builds on Directive 90/386/EEC for definitions, with some additional definitions, including national regulatory authority. 

Member States must ensure that information regarding leased lines, offerings on technical characteristics, tariffs, supply and usage conditions, licensing and declaration requirements, and the conditions for the attachment of terminal equipment is published. The Directive described which information is to be supplied.

Access to and usage of leased lines may be restricted only for ensuring compliance with the essential requirements, compatible with Community law, and imposed by the national regulatory authorities through regulatory means. Essential requirements shall apply in regards to security of network operations, maintenance of network integrity, interoperability of services, and data protection. 

Member States must inform the Commission on the identity of the national authority (again symbolizing it is no longer controlled by telecommunications administrations). Authorities must provide statistical reports and case details on restrictions of leased lines, especially due to alleged infringement of rights or resale prohibitions, including measures taken and their reasons.

Member States must also inform the Commission if they foresee that they will not be able to fulfill the requirements regarding the minimum provision of leased lines.

The Directive also set a right to any user that complain an injury by the infringement of the Directive and a right to appeal to the national regulatory authority. If they cannot reach an agreement with the authority, the user can invoke a designated procedure with the ONP committee.

The Commission must report to the Parliament and Council.
column17:
The Directive operationalises self-regulation by allowing telecommunications organisations to make initial compliance and enforcement decisions, including refusing, interrupting, or limiting leased line services for alleged breaches of usage conditions. However, these measures are subject to procedural oversight and approval by the national regulatory authority, which establishes the procedures, authorises certain actions, and reviews requests to depart from published supply conditions.

Member States must ensure that the national regulatory authority establishes procedures to decide, on a case-by-case basis and as quickly as possible, whether to allow or deny telecommunications organizations the right to take actions such as refusing to provide a leased line, interrupting leased line services, or reducing leased line features. These decisions are based on suspected violations of usage conditions by leased line users. The procedures may also include provisions for the authority to pre-approve certain measures for specific violations of usage rules.
Member States shall ensure that these procedures provide for a transparent decision-making process in which due respect is given to the rights of the parties. 
The national regulatory authority shall ensure that telecommunications organizations adhere to the principle of non-discrimination when they make use of the public telecommunications network for providing services which are or may be provided also by other service providers. When telecommunications organizations use leased lines for the provision of services not covered by special and/or exclusive rights, the same type of leased lines must be provided to other users on request and under equal conditions.

3. Where, in response to a particular request, a telecommunications organization considers it unreasonable to provide a leased line under its published tariffs and supply conditions, it must seek seek the agreement of the national regulatory authority to vary those conditions in that case.
column20: Telecommunications organisations make initial decisions about alleged violations of usage conditions and may refuse, interrupt or restrict leased-line services, subject to transparent procedures and NRA oversight. This places them between the regulator and leased-line users

The main intermediaries are collecting societies, which manage and exercise retransmission rights collectively, and mediators, which facilitate contractual negotiations between rightholders and cable operators.

column4: Council Directive 93/97/EEC of 29 October 1993 supplementing Directive 91/263/EEC in respect of satellite earth station equipments

The directive empowers member states to regulate satellite earth station equipment  by taking appropriate measures to ensure that receive-only satellite earth station equipment not intended for terrestrial connection to the public telecommunications network may be placed on the market and put into service and used on their territory, in conformity with national law compatible with Community law, only if it complies with the requirements of this Directive. They must also ensure that equipmentquiptment not intended for terrestrial connection to the public telecommunications network is not permitted to be connected to the public telecommunications network.
They are not allowed to impede the circulation of equiptment aligning with the directive.
They must presume conformity when the equipment conforms toequiptment confirm with national standards. 

The Commission is responsible for identifying categories of satellite earth station equipment that require common technical regulations and mandating the preparation of corresponding harmonised standards by the relevant standardisation bodies. Once these standards are developed, the Commission adopts them as mandatory common technical regulations and publishes their references in the Official Journal.e

Where either the Commission or a member states considers that an harmonised standard exceed or do not entirely meet the relevant requirements, it will notify the committee established under directive 91/263/EEC.

Manufacturers of earth station equiptment must satify the requiremetns set in Directive 91/263/EEC.
column17:

When it comes to receive-only earth station equiptment, manufacturers can choose between conformity assessmnet based on Article 9(1) and (2) of Directive 91/263/EEC or Community internal production control procedures set out in the Annex, as far the requirements of this Directive are concerned.

Internal procedures are conformity assessment whereby the manufacturer ensures and declares that the products satify the requirements. The manufacturer must establish the technical documentation and must keep it for 10 years for the disposal of the relevant national authorities. The documentation include general description, conceptual design and manufacturing drawings, descreption and explanations necessary for the understanding of the drawings, and a list of standards mentioned in Article 5 applied in full or as far as is relevant or, in the absence of such standards, the technical construction file, and descriptions of the solutions adopted to meet those requirements, as well as result of design calculations and test report

column16:
The Decision establishes an EU Action Plan for the Introduction of Advanced Television Services in Europe (1993–1997). Through financial incentives for broadcasters and programme producers, it aims to accelerate the deployment of 16:9 advanced television services, stimulate programme production, and promote market uptake of advanced television technologies across the EU.

The European Commission implements the action plan, assisted by a committee of Member State representatives, while Member States participate in oversight through the committee procedures.
column17: The Decision operationalises self-regulation by making public funding contingent on private initiative and co-financing. Broadcasters, programme producers, and other market actors design projects, secure private financial commitments, and implement services, while the Commission evaluates proposals and allocates funding according to predefined criteria.

column16:
The Directive amends Commission Directive 88/301/EEC and Commission Directive 90/388/EEC.
It mostly represent the current situation of the regime. The goal of achiving the full liberalisation of the satellite and equipment sectors, including the abolition of all exclusive or special nights in this area, subject to licensing procedures, as well as for the free unrestricted access to space segment capacity. The goal of this Directive is to create the environment to enable existing constraints to be removed and new activities developed in the field of satellite communications, while stressing the need to harmonize and liberalize the markets in satellite equipment and services.

It especially notes that several Member States have already opened up certain satellite communications services to competition and have introduced licensing schemes. Nevertheless, the granting of licences in some Member States still does not follow objective, proportional and non-discriminatory criteria or, in the case of operators competing with the telecommunications organizations, is subject to technical restrictions such as a ban on connecting their equipment to be switched network operated by the telecommunications organization. Other Member States have maintained the exclusive rights granted to the national public undertakings.

Commission Directive 88/301/EC aimed to abolish the special and exclusive rights in telecommunications terminal equipment, but it does not cover all types of satellite earth station equipment.

Exclusive rights restrict the free movement of telecommunications equipment by limiting importation, marketing, connection, and maintenance, as monopolies lack incentives to service or price competitively without market threats. Since many markets feature diverse telecommunication products and limited manufacturers, any right that restricts authorized importers or service providers—such as by denying open, non-discriminatory procedures—can effectively act like exclusive rights.

Exclusive or special rights acting as measures similar to quantitative restrictions are incompatible with Article 30 of the EC Treaty. The features of satellite earth stations and their market do not justify different legal treatment from other telecom equipment. Therefore, all exclusive rights related to import, marketing, connection, service, and maintenance of satellite earth station equipment, along with similar rights—except legal or regulatory advantages affecting only certain undertakings—must be abolished. These rights limit other operators' ability to operate under similar conditions in the same area.

1. Background

1.1. With the adoption of its Communication "1992 Review of the Situation in the Telecommunications Services Sector" of 21 October 1992 (SEC(92) 1048 final), the Commission launched a wide-ranging debate about the development of the telecommunications sector in the European Community.

1.2. The purpose of this review and the proposals it contains is to initiate further progress towards the complete liberalization of the public telecommunications service within the European Community.

1.3. The starting point is the 1987 Green Paper on the Development of the Common Market for Telecommunications Services and Equipment. Since then the Commission's policy has been to bring about the single internal market for telecommunications services through liberalization and harmonization.

1.4. Article 10 of Directive 90/388/EEC of 28 June 1990 on competition in the market for telecommunications services states that during 1992 the Commission "will carry out an overall assessment of the situation in the telecommunications sector in relation to the aims of this Directive."

1.5. On the basis of studies and analyses of the prospects for the telecommunications sector up to the year 2010, the review identifies the various opportunities for further liberalization. Besides the main review, four options for future action are proposed in a separate section.

2. Summary of the Commission Communication

2.1. The Communication of 21 October 1992 (SEC(92) 1048 final) reviews technical and economic developments, EC telecommunications policy to date and the international situation in this sector.

2.2. An assessment of the current situation points up the positive results, but also the difficulties and bottlenecks in implementing the earlier regulations with regard to tariffs, traffic diversion, delays in the offering of new networks and services, etc.

2.3. Four proposals (options) are put forward as objectives specific to telecommunications, along with some complementary actions.

2.4. Finally, the Commission proposed proceeding to a broad consultation with all the interested parties, giving them a chance to air their views prior to a final Council decision on future action.

4. The Council Resolution on the review of the situation of the telecommunications sector and the need for further development in that market

4.1. At its meeting on 16 June 1993 the Council of Ministers adopted, on the basis of the Commission proposal, a Resolution setting out the key aspects of future regulatory policy and the main short- and long-term objectives.

4.2. The following major goals in the short term were specified:
Adoption of legislative proposals regarding the introduction of Open Network Provision (ONP) and satellites, together with the rapid and effective application of existing Community legislation in telecommunications services and ONP.
Implementation and, where necessary, recognition of ONP principles in relation to future liberalization, universal service, network interconnection, access charges, and licensing conditions.
Development of future Community policy on mobile and personal communications, supported by the publication of a Green Paper on mobile communications.
Development of future Community policy on telecommunications infrastructure and cable TV networks, supported by a Green Paper on this subject.
Measures to address problems affecting peripheral regions and less developed networks, complementing national funding and making appropriate use of Community support.
Consideration of the particular situation of small networks when preparing implementing measures.
4.3. The following major objectives in the long term were also specified:
Liberalization of all public voice telephony services while maintaining universal service.
Maintaining a balance between liberalization and harmonization in a growing market.
Examination of progress in structural adjustment, particularly tariff adjustment in countries facing particular difficulties, with additional transitional periods where necessary.
Formulation of a future policy for telecommunications infrastructure based on the results of consultation following publication of the Green Paper on infrastructure.
4.4. The Council also calls on the Member States:
To promote the progressive approximation of tariffs towards cost orientation while continuing to develop universal service at reasonable prices.
To provide telecommunications organizations with the necessary financial, organizational and management independence to prepare for competition.
4.5. The Committee supports the following target dates proposed by the Commission:
Publication of a Green Paper on mobile communications by 1 January 1994.
Publication of a Green Paper on telecommunications infrastructure and cable TV networks by 1 January 1995.
Necessary amendments to the Community framework by 1 January 1996 to enable full liberalization of public voice telephony services by 1 January 1998.
Transitional measures of up to five years for Member States with less developed networks requiring structural adjustment.
Commission reports by the end of 1993 on an internationally comprehensible EC telecommunications policy framework and by the end of 1994 on implementation progress and its impact.

The Directive governs the harmonisation of conditions for open network provision (ONP) in voice telephony. It seeks to guarantee universal access to fixed public telephone networks, ensure transparency, non-discrimination, quality of service, fair tariffs, interoperability, and user protection while supporting the gradual liberalisation of telecommunications markets.

Member States implement the Directive through national law, ensure that telecommunications organisations provide the required services, designate and empower national regulatory authorities, notify the Commission of the relevant organisations and authorities, and ensure effective enforcement of the Directive.

National regulatory authorities (NRAs) are the principal regulators. They supervise market conduct, approve or review tariffs and cost accounting, oversee quality of service, numbering, contracts, access conditions, interconnection, dispute resolution, transparency obligations, publication requirements, and restrictions on access and use. They also supervise agreements between telecommunications organisations and intervene where necessary.

The Commission provides overall coordination and oversight. It requests European standards where appropriate, monitors implementation and convergence, publishes notifications received from Member States, reviews the functioning of the Directive, and may recommend or adopt measures to promote Community-wide convergence.

The NRAs need to set and publish targets for the supply-time and quality-of-service indicators, ensure that service offerings continue for a reasonable period of time and that termination of an offering, and that users have a contract which specifies the service to be provided by a telecommunications organization. They can require alternation of the conditions of contracts and the conditions of any compensation and/or refund schemes used by telecommunications organizations.
They also have to agree to a request by a telecommunications organization to change the conditions for the provision of a connection to the fixed public telephone network under its published tariffs and supply conditions. They must also ensure that telecommunications organizations respond to reasonable requests for access to the fixed public telephone network at network termination points. While Technical and commercial arrangements for special network access shall be a matter for agreement between the parties involved, the NAR may intervene, for example, to set conditions that are non discriminatory, are fair and reasonable for both parties and offer the greatest benefit to all users.
NRAs may also require that the agreements include conditions that meet the criteria set out in paragraph 3, are entered into and implemented in an efficient and timely manner and include conditions on conformity with relevant standards, compliance with essential requirements and/or the maintenance of end-to-end quality.

NRA are also tasked with overseeing interconnection, and allow telecommunication organsations to refuse an interconnection request.  They may also intervene in technical and commercial arrangements for interconnection shall be a matter for agreement between the parties involved.

They must ensure that tariffes follow he basic principles of transparency and cost orientation, and may place constraints to the objectives of universal telephone-service accessibility.

column16:
The directive regulates the way member states issue licenses and set conditions for providers of telecommunication services. These licenses can be in the form of individual licenses or as general authorisation, meaning a class license which does not require an organisation to obtain an explicit decision by an authority.
The conditions member states must abide are listed in the annex and must be applied objectively justified in relation to the service concerned. Member states should issue individual licenses only where the beneficiary receive access to scarce resources or is suject to particular obligations or enjoys particular rights.

Additionally, member states must publish conditions in an appropriate mannter so to provide easy access to that information. They are permitted to amend them in objectively justified cases. Conditions to general authorisations are also listed in the annex. Member states however can require undertaking which complies with the conditions to notify the regulatory authority of its intention to provide telecommunications services and communicate the relevant information relating the service that is necessary for the purpose of ensuring compliance with the conditions. The authority may inform undertaking that they do not comply and it is not entited to avail itself of the general authorisation. It may impose on the undertaking porportionate specific measures aimed at ensuring compliance. The undertaking should also given a reasonable opportunity to state its views on the application of the conditions and to remedy any breach within one month, and then the authority can then annul or modify the decision as appropriate and state the reasons for its decision. The undertaking may apeal decisions to an independent institutions. 

Fees for authoritisation, may only cover administrative costs incurred in issuing, managing, controling, and enforcing the applicable general authorisation scheme. They must be appropriate and sufficently detailed manner.

Member state may issue individual liceneses only for specific purposes, for instance to allow access to radio frequncies, to provide particular rights to access lands, to impose obligations and requirements relating to the mandatory provision of publicly available telecommunications services, or to impose specific obligations on actors with significant market powers. The conditions for individual licenses are also set in the Annex, and they must not restrict or complement by any conditions attached to general authorisation unless it is objectively justified and proportionate.
The granting of individual liceneses must be made through open, non-discriminatory and transparent procedures, and should have reasonable time limits.
Any undertaking which fulfils the conditions decided and published by the member states shall be entitiled to receive an individual licenese. When the do not fulfill the conditions imposed, the regulatory authority may withdraw, amend, or suspend the individual license or impose proportionate and specific measures aimed at ensuring compliance. The MS must inform the undertaking for its reasons to withdraw, amend, or suspend an individual license. 
Member states may limit the number of individual licenses for any category only to the extent required to ensure the efficinet use of radio frequencies. They must give due weight to the need to maximize benefit for users, develop competition, enable interested parties to express their views, publish its decision and reasons, review the limitation at reasonable intervals, and invite applications. Member States shall grant such individual licences on the basis of selection criteria which must be objective, non-discriminatoriy, detailed, transparent and proportionate.

MS may adopt provisional conditions allowing providers of new services not yet covered by a general authorisation  to starting providing services or reject the application with reasonable cause. It then must adopt defintive conditions or consent to the provision of the service concerned.
