The aim of this Directive, replacing Directive 95/62, is to harmonize the conditions for open and efficient access to and use of fixed public telephone networks and fixed public telephone services in an environment of open and competitive markets (market liberalisation).

Member States are responsible for implementing the Directive and ensuring the provision of universal service, while national regulatory authorities (NRAs) are responsible for supervising telecommunications markets and enforcing the Directive's regulatory requirements.

Member States must ensure that specific services are available to all users in their territories, and if they cannot be provided commercially, they may set up funding schemes for shared financing of these services. These services include directory services, public pay telephones, and services for disabled users and users with special social needs. They must ensure that all users with a connection to the fixed public telephone network can: (a) connect and use terminal equipment in accordance with national and Community law; (b) access operator assistance and directory enquiry services unless the subscriber opts out; (c) reach emergency services at no cost using dialling code "112" or other codes set by national regulators.

National regulatory authorities (NRAs) are the primary regulators, overseeing implementation, designating universal service providers, monitoring quality and tariffs, resolving disputes, supervising undertakings with significant market power, and enforcing compliance.
National regulatory authorities ensure that all regulated organisations provide a contract as described in Article 10. They may request alterations to the contract either on their own initiative or in response to a request from an organization representing users or consumers. They also ensure that organisations publish adequate and up-to-date information for consumers on their standard terms and conditions, and that organisations with significant market power publish performance information based on the prescribed parameters, definitions and measurement methods. National regulatory authorities shall be able to require independent audits of this performance data to ensure its accuracy and comparability (Article 12.4).

National regulatory authorities must also establish transparent procedures for addressing situations in which organisations interrupt, terminate, materially vary, or reduce the availability of services to organisations that provide telecommunications networks and/or services. They may impose essential requirements regarding the security of network operations, network maintenance, interoperability, data protection, and the effective use of the frequency spectrum. They may also require organisations with significant market power to provide the facilities described in the Annex and satisfy reasonable requests from organisations providing telecommunications services for access to the fixed public telephone network.

The Directive states that national regulatory authorities should assume that an organisation has significant market power if it holds at least a 25% market share. They may also determine that an organisation with less than 25% market share has significant market power, or that an organisation with more than 25% market share does not.

The European Commission develops implementing measures, monitors the Directive's implementation, receives notifications from Member States, and may review or amend technical requirements. Member States must notify the Commission of organisations designated as having significant market power. The Commission monitors implementation of these provisions and may request national regulatory authorities to justify why an organisation has, or has not, been classified as having significant market power.

(1) Since 1 January 1998, with transition periods for some Member States, telecom services and infrastructure in the Community will be liberalised. The Council, European Parliament, Economic and Social Committee, and Committee of the Regions agree that liberalisation must be accompanied by a harmonised regulatory framework to ensure universal service.
column17:
Telecommunications organisations implement many operational obligations within this regulatory framework. The Directive operationalises self-regulation by allowing telecommunications organisations to determine many commercial and operational matters within the regulatory framework. While these decisions remain subject to transparency requirements and, where specified, oversight or intervention by national regulatory authorities, the day-to-day organization and administration of telecommunications services are largely delegated to the regulated organisations themselves.

Organisations determine subscriber contracts, service conditions, tariffs and discount schemes, publish commercial and quality-of-service information, establish cost-accounting systems, negotiate network access agreements, provide additional facilities beyond the minimum requirements, determine procedures for service interruption or termination, and may request compensation for universal service obligations or approval to depart from published supply conditions in individual cases. 

Organisations designated as having significant market power assume additional responsibilities, including maintaining cost-oriented tariffs, operating transparent cost-accounting systems, publishing performance information, providing non-discriminatory network access, and satisfying reasonable access requests from other telecommunications organisations.
column18:
Indirectly mentioned:
organisation representing user or consumer interests (article 10 & Article 26(c)(1))

Independent auditors (Article 12.4)

Independent dispute resolution bodies (Article 26(c)(1)) 

The Directive introduces several regulatory intermediaries who support oversight, representation, and dispute resolution. Organisations representing users and consumers participate in regulatory oversight by requesting amendments to subscriber contracts. Independent auditors verify the accuracy and comparability of performance information published by organisations with significant market power. Independent dispute resolution bodies provide accessible mechanisms for resolving disputes between users and telecommunications organisations outside the courts. These actors do not regulate directly, but facilitate representation, monitoring, and enforcement within the regulatory framework.
column21: Auditors and dispute resolution bodies must be independent

column4: Directive relating to telecommunications terminal equipment and satellite earth station equipment, including the mutual recognition of their conformity
column16:
The Directive directly regulates manufacturers of telecommunications terminal equipment (Title I) and satellite earth station equipment (Title II). 

Regulatory authority is exercised primarily by Member States, which are responsible for market surveillance, CE-marking enforcement, withdrawal of non-compliant equipment, licensing where applicable, and ensuring compliance with the Directive's requirements.

The Commission performs coordination and rule-making functions, including the adoption of measures concerning common technical regulations, consultation with relevant parties, and the management of procedures concerning harmonised standards. A designated committee advises on whether harmonised standards satisfy the essential requirements of the Directive.

Relevant standardisation bodies prepare the harmonised standards referenced by the Directive. 

Notified bodies and test laboratories act as regulatory intermediaries within the conformity-assessment procedures, while manufacturers remain responsible for demonstrating conformity with the Directive's requirements.

For the regulation of telecommunications terminal equiptment (Title I):
The directive directly regulates manufacturers placing equiptment on the market. Terminal equiptment must follow essential requirements, including ensuring safety of employees of public telecommunications network operators, electromagnetic compatibility requirements, protection of the network from harm, effective use of the radio frequency spectrum, interworking of terminal equiptment  with network equiptment, and interworking of terminal equipment via the public telecommunications network.

Member States are the primary regulators under both titles. Members states must take all appropriate measure to ensure that equiptment may be placed on the market and put into service inf they bear the CE markting attesting conformity with the directive and their disconnection when it does not used for its intended purposes.
Member states shall not prevent the placing on the market of equipment that complies with the directive, and shall presume compliance with the essential requirements when there is an alignment with national standards referenced in the OJEC.
Member states need to inform the Commission if it considers that harmonised standards do not meet the essential requirements, in which case a designated committee shall deliver its opinion.

IF the member state finds that a terminal equiptment does not comply with the essential requirements, it shall take appropriate measures to withdraw the products from the market and immediatly inform the Commission of any measures and the reasons for non-compliance. It will also inform the Commission of Commission of the measures taken and indicate the reasons for its decision, and in particular whether the non-compliance is due to incorrect application of harmonised standards/common technical regulations, or shortcoming with the standards or technical regulations.
Where the Member state finds that the CE marking was affixed improperly, the manufacturer shall make the equiptment conform with the provisions concerning the CE marking and end the infridgement.

The role of the commission is to adopt measures to identify the type of terminal equipment for which a common technical regulation is required, as well as the corresponding harmonized standards prepared by the relevant standardization bodies, implementing the essential requirements, which shall be transformed into common technical regulations, compliance with which shall be mandatory.
The Commission is also tasked with entering into consulation with relevant parties, and if the issue is with standards or common specifications, it will inform the relevant committee. 

Relevant standardization bodies prepare the harmonized standards referenced by the Directive and used by the Commission when adopting common technical regulations.

Notified bodies act as regulatory intermediaries by carrying out the conformity-assessment functions established under the Directive. Test laboratories support these procedures through technical testing but do not themselves certify conformity.

Notified bodies may request manufacturers to justify the intended purpose of such equipment on the basis of its relevant technical characteristics, its functions and indications of the market segment it is intended for.

For the regulation of satellite earth station equiptment (title II):
Manufacturers of satellite earth station equipment are the regulated entites under this title. They must declare whether the equipment is intended or not intended for terrestrial connection to the public telecommunications network. The equiptment must satify similar requirements as the requirements set in title I, with the needed changes as described in article 17. 

Member states must take appropriate measures to ensure that receive-only satellite earth station equipment not intended for terrestrial connection to the public telecommunications network may be placed on the market and put into service and used on their territory comply with national law. They must take all appropriate measures to ensure that other satellite earth station equiptment  may be placed on the market only if it complies with the requirements of this Directive when it is properly installed and maintained and used for its intended purposes. They may license such use.
They must ensure that that satellite earth station equipment which is not intended for terrestrial connection to the public telecommunications network is not permitted to be connected to the public telecommunications network.
They mustl also not impede the free circulation and the placing on the market of satelite earth station equiptment.
They will presume conformity when manufacturers align with national standards. 
Member states must ensure that CE marking the might confuse would not be allowed.
And the same procedures set for failure to fulfiling the obligations of manufacturers under title I, applies for title II.

The Commission, designated committee, and relevant standardisation bodies perform the same functions under Title II as under Title I regarding common technical regulations, harmonised standards, and consultation procedures.

Conformity assessment under title II aligns with conformity assessment under title I, but in addition when the satellite earth station equipment which is not intended for connection to the public telecommunications network shall be accompanied by a manufacturer's or supplier's declaration made and transmitted in accordance with the same procedures as those set out in Article 3 and Annex VIII.

The roles and procedures of notified bodies and test laboratories are the same as those established under Title I, with notified bodies performing conformity-assessment functions and test laboratories providing technical testing support.
column17:
This is a process-based regulation enhanced through third-party assurance. Manufacturers retain responsibility for compliance and may choose between different conformity-assessment routes, but these routes rely extensively on notified-body involvement. Test laboratories provide technical testing support within these procedures.


For the regulation of telecommunications terminal equiptment (Title I):
Manufacturers remain responsible for demonstrating conformity and may choose between different conformity-assessment routes, including the EC type-examination route under Annex I and the full quality-assurance route under Annex IV.

Under Annex I, a notified body carries out an EC type-examination and certifies that a representative product complies with the Directive's requirements. Following type-examination, the manufacturer must either issue a declaration of conformity to type under Annex II or operate an approved production quality-assurance system under Annex III. Annex III requires a notified body to assess and monitor the manufacturer's quality system.

Alternatively, Annex IV establishes a full quality-assurance procedure. Under this route, the manufacturer operates an approved quality system for design, manufacture, and final inspection and testing, which must be assessed and approved by a notified body and remains subject to notified-body surveillance.

Where the Member state finds that the CE marking was affixed improperly, the manufacturer shall make the equiptment conform with the provisions concerning the CE marking and end the infridgement.

Self-regulation is therefore operationalised through manufacturer responsibility for demonstrating conformity and selecting among alternative conformity-assessment pathways. However, the Directive does not appear to provide a purely self-assessment route. Instead, both the type-examination route (Annexes I-III) and the full quality-assurance route (Annex IV) incorporate notified-body involvement.

Self-regulation is enhanced via notified bodies, which the member states designate for carrying out the certification, product checks and associated surveillance tasks pertaining to the procedures. Annex V describes the minimum criteria for designation.

Under Annex I, notified bodies certify conformity through EC type-examination. Under Annex III, they assess and supervise production quality-assurance systems. They also carry out product checks and surveillance activities under the relevant procedures.

Under Annex IV, they assess, approve, and supervise full quality-assurance systems. They also carry out product checks and surveillance activities under the relevant procedures. Annex IV establishes a notified-body-supervised quality-assurance regime. Manufacturers operate an approved quality system and declare conformity, while notified bodies assess, approve, monitor, audit, and periodically inspect the system to ensure continued compliance. EN ISO 9001 operates as a harmonised benchmark: it is not mandatory, but its implementation creates a presumption that the manufacturer's quality system satisfies Annex IV's requirements.

Test laboratories enhance the regime by performing the technical tests and measurements used to assess compliance with the Directive's requirements. Unlike notified bodies, they do not certify conformity or supervise manufacturers. Rather, they generate the technical evidence that manufacturers and notified bodies may rely upon during conformity assessment.

For the regulation of satellite earth station equipment (Title II), the conformity-assessment structure is broadly the same. Manufacturers remain responsible for demonstrating conformity and may rely on the same conformity-assessment procedures, while notified bodies and test laboratories perform the same certification, assessment, surveillance, and testing functions. The principal differences concern the specific requirements applicable to satellite earth station equipment, particularly regarding connection to public telecommunications networks and the additional manufacturer's or supplier's declaration required for certain equipment.
column21:
Annex V establishes the minimum criteria for the designation of notified bodies, including requirements for independence, competence, impartiality, resources, liability, and confidentiality.

Member States designate test laboratories to perform conformity testing, but unlike notified bodies, laboratories are not subject to the Annex V criteria. Instead, they must comply with the relevant harmonized standards, which notified bodies apply when relying on laboratory testing during conformity assessment. So the laboratory is not a subordinate of the notified body, but an independent entity designated by the Member State under a different set of criteria. This separation explains why the Directive includes two distinct designation regimes.

column4: Directive 98/48/EC amending Directive 98/34/EC laying down a procedure for the provision of information in the field of technical standards and regulations
column16:
The Directive amends Directive 98/34/EC to adapt it also for the provision of information in the field of technical standards and regulations and of rules on information society services. It adds a definition of a service to address any information society service that is to say, any service normally provided for remuneration, at a distance, by electronic means and at the individual request of a recipient of services. This amendment excludes radio and television broadcasting services (as the latter are regulated by Directive 89/552/EEC). 

It also adds a definition for technical regulations, which includes a definition for de-facto technical regulations encompassing professional codes or codes of practice which in turn refer to technical specifications or to other requirements or to rules on services, compliance with which confers a presumption of conformity with the obligations imposed by the aforementioned laws, regulations or administrative provisions. 

The amendment therefore recognises professional bodies and other organisations developing codes of practice as governance actors where compliance with their codes confers a presumption of conformity with legal obligations.

Directive 98/34/EC sets several regulatory bodies:
Member States must notify draft technical regulations before their adoption and participate in the exchange of information concerning technical standards, technical regulations, and rules affecting the internal market.
IF the member state finds that a terminal equiptment does not comply with the essential requirements, it shall take appropriate measures to withdraw the products from the market and immediatly inform the Commission of any measures and the reasons for non-compliance.

The Commission occupies a central coordination role by receiving and distributing notifications, reviewing draft measures, and coordinating the information procedure established by the Directive.

The Directive also recognises several standardisation bodies. At the European level, these include CEN, Cenelec, and ETSI, while national standards bodies are responsible for adopting, preparing, and communicating standards within the notification system.

The Directive therefore combines state oversight with a formal role for standardisation bodies, which act as intermediary actors in the development, dissemination, and coordination of technical standards.
column17:
Self-regulation is operationalised through prescriptive rules embodied in professional codes and codes of practice.

For Directive 98/34/EC, self-regulation is operationalised through prescriptive standards and technical specifications developed by recognised standardisation bodies. These standards define the characteristics or requirements of products and services and serve as reference points for regulatory harmonisation.
column18: Professional bodies and other organisations developing codes of practice

column4: Green Paper on Radio Spectrum Policy: in the context of European Community policies such as telecommunication, broadcasting, transport, and R&D
Radio and Telecommunications Terminal Equipment Directive (R&TTE)
column16:
The Directive regulates telecommunications apparatus, ensuring the protection of people's health and safety, electromagenetic compatibility contained in Directive 89/336/EEC, the effective use of the allocated spectrum for radio communication, support features ensuring avoidance of fraud, support emergency services, and facilitate the use of appartus by people with disabilities. 

Appartus that meet relevant harmonised standards published in the OJEC are presummed to be in compliance

Regulatory authority is assigned primarily to the Member States, which ensure that appartus comply with the requirements and that providers supply the required information to users. They also must permit the placing on the market and putting into service of apparatus that comply with the requirements, but may restrict this  only for reasons related to the effective and appropriate use of the radio spectrum, avoidance of harmful interference or matters relating to public health. They should ensure that operatiots of public telecommunications networks do not refuse to connect terminal equiptment that comply with the requirements, unless the operator considers that an appartus causes serious damage to a network or harmful radio interference or harm the network or its functioning.
Member states should also not prohibit, restrict, or impede the placing on the market of apprtus that bear the CE marking indicating conformity.
If a member state finds that an appartus does not comply with the requirements, it shall take appropriate measures to withdraw it.
The Member States need also to take appropriate actions against people who affix a EC marking but not in compliance with the requirement and the conformity assessment procedures. 


The Commission's task is to maintain a record of all the cases notified by the Member States of non-compliance. The Commission also publishes references to harmonised standards in the Official Journal and receives notifications concerning designated notified bodies.
The Commission is tasked with entering into consultation with the parties involved in cases of non-compliance, and if the issues relates to the shortcommings of harmonised standards or common technical regulation, it should inform the relevant committee (no longer ACTE, but rather the Telecommunication Conformity Assessment and Market Surveillance Committee (TCAM)).

The Directive also allows Member States to notify the Commission on the designation of notifed bodies to carry out tasks associated with assessing conformity. Notified bodies act as regulatory intermediaries within the conformity-assessment system. Member States are responsible for designating, monitoring, and, where necessary, withdrawing the designation of notified bodies, while the Commission publicises their designation.


The Directive establishes a transition period for standards recognized under previous directives, including Directive 89/336/EEC.
column17:
Manufacturers can decide how to achieve and demonstate compliance with the requirements. They may adopt harmonised standards to benefit from a presumption of conformity, and Article 10 describes different conformity-assessment procedures depending on whether harmonised standards are fully applied, partly applied, or not applied. 
Self-regulation is operationalised through manufacturer responsibility for conformity assessment. 

The Directive permits reliance on internal production control (Article 10(3)), where manufacturers apply the relevant harmonised standards in full. In these cases, they may demonstrate conformity without involving a notified body. Under Annex III, the manufacturer self-assesses, keeps technical documentation, and declares conformity.

Self-regulation is enhanced through notified bodies (Article 10(4) or 10(5)) where harmonised standards are not applied, are applied only in part, or where the relevant procedures require additional third-party assessment. In these cases, notified bodies provide an additional conformity-assessment layer while responsibility for compliance remains with the manufacturer.
Annex IV applies when harmonised standards are absent, partly used, or not used. Manufacturer prepares a technical file; a notified body reviews it. Under Annex IV, a notified body reviews the technical construction file and issues an opinion on conformity.
Annex V offers an alternative route where notified body assesses and supervises the manufacturer’s quality-assurance system. Under Annex V, the manufacturer operates a full quality-assurance system that is assessed and monitored by a notified body.

The regime therefore combines standards-based and process-based self-regulation. Regulated entities retain discretion over how to achieve compliance and may choose between alternative conformity-assessment pathways, while harmonised standards provide a voluntary route to demonstrating conformity.

Annex VI explains the minimum requirements for designating notified bodies, which include independence, technical competence, professional integrity, and adequate resources to perform conformity-assessment tasks.

Notified bodies do not replace manufacturer responsibility for compliance. Rather, they provide third-party assessment within a system in which the primary responsibility for demonstrating conformity remains with the regulated entity.

column4: Directive on a Community framework for electronic signatures
column16:
The Directive directly regulates certification-service providers that issue qualified certificates to the public, as well as providers of certification services more generally. These providers must comply with the requirements set out in Annex II, including obligations relating to reliability, identity verification, security, record-keeping, liability, and data protection.

Member States are the primary regulators. They must ensure supervision of certification-service providers established in their territory that issue qualified certificates to the public, establish or maintain voluntary accreditation schemes where desired, designate bodies responsible for accreditation and supervision, and ensure the free movement of certification services and electronic-signature products within the internal market.

Member states are given direct regulatory authority, yet they are not permitted to subject certification services to prior authorisation. They can introduce or maintain voluntary accreditation schemes to enhance the levels of certification-service provision. These accreditation schemes must be objective, transparent, proportionate, and non-discriminatory. 
The member states must ensure the establishment of approprirate systems for supervising certification-service-providers, and conformity of the signature-creation-devices with the requirements laid in the Annex will be determined by either public or private bodies, and all member states must recognized said determination of conformity. In the public sector, member state may set additional requirements for electronic signatures, and they must be objective, transparent, proportionate and non-discriminatory and shall relate only to the specific characteristics of the application concerned.

Member states are requires to apply the national provision which they adopt to certification-service-providers and may not restrict the provision of similar services originating in another member states. They must ensure that electronic signature products can circulate freely. They must ensure that advanced electronic signatures which are based on qualified certificated statify legal requirements of a signature in the same manner as handwritten signatures and are administable as evidence in legal proceedings.

The Commission performs coordination, standardisation, and implementation functions. It receives notifications from the MS on voluntary accreditation schemes, the names and address of nation bodies responsible for accreditation and supervision, and the names of accredited national certification service providers. It also reviews the operation of the directive and its scope. It can also establish and publish references to generally recognized standards for electronic-signature products, and the member states must presume compliance when electronic signature products meet these standards.

It may establish criteria for the designation of conformity-assessment bodies, publish references to generally recognised standards for electronic-signature products, promote the development and use of signature-verification devices, facilitate international recognition of certification services, and oversee implementation of the Directive.

The Commission is assisted by a designated committee.
column17:
The Directive operationalises self-regulation through proces-based regulation through liability regime, enhanced though voluntary accreditation schemes and the possibility of private-sector-based supervision of certification-service providers. Certification-service providers are not subject to prior authorisation and may choose whether to participate in accreditation schemes designed to promote higher levels of trust, security, and service quality.

Self-regulation is further perationalised by requiring certification-service providers issuing qualified certificates to develop and maintain internal organisational, technical, security, record-keeping, liability-management, and quality-control systems that satisfy the requirements of Annex II. Providers themselves remain responsible for demonstrating compliance with these requirements.

Self-regulation is established via a liability regime where certification-service-providers are liable for damages caused to any entity or legal/natural person who reasonably relies on the certificates, especially in regards to the accuracy of all the information contained in the certificates, the assurances regarding that the signatory identified in the certficate held the signature-creating data and the assurance that the signature-creation data and the signature-verification data can be used in a complementary manner in cases where the certification-service-provider generates them both. All, as long as the provider can proves that the has not acted neligently. 

The regime is enhanced through accreditation, supervision, and conformity assessment. Member States may establish voluntary accreditation schemes, public or private supervisory systems, and designate public or private bodies to assess whether secure signature-creation devices comply with Annex III.
column18:
Two actors act as intermediaries:
National bodies responsible for accreditation and supervision oversee certification-service providers and any voluntary accreditation schemes established under national law.

Public or private conformity-assessment bodies for secure signature-creation devices. They are designated by Member States and assess the conformity of secure signature-creation devices with the requirements of Annex III. Their conformity determinations must be recognised throughout the Union.
column21: Certification service providers and national bodies responsible for accreditation or supervision must comply with the rules on data protection set in the EDPD, especially with regard to collecting information directly from data subjects and with their consent.

column4: Decision on the coordinated introduction of a third-generation mobile and wireless communications system (UMTS) in the Community
column16:
The Decision regulates the introduction of compatible UMTS networks and services, meaning third-generation mobile and wireless communications systems. The Decision requires the MS to take necessary actions to coordinate and progress the introduction of UMTS services and to allow organisations providing UMTS networks to negotiate cross-border roaming agreements. The Member States also need to provide the Commission with information required for verifying the implementation of the Decision.

The Commission is empowered to negotiate with CEPT and two of its sub-committees on the harmonization of frequency use. It may also cooperate with ETSI to promote a common and open standard for the provision of compatible UMTS services throughout Europe taking into account the need to present a common standard to the ITU as an option for the worldwide ITU IMT 2000 recommendation. Beyond that, the Commission may seek the implementation of international agreements applicable to UMTS, and shall, in particular and where necessary, submit proposals to the Council for appropriate mandates for the negotiation of bilateral and multilateral agreements with third countries and international organisations.
column17: The Decision requires the MS to take necessary actions to coordinate and progress the introduction of UMTS services and to allow organisations providing UMTS networks to negotiate cross-border roaming agreements.

column4: Communication on the Organisation and Management of the Internet International and European Policy Issues 1998- 2000
column16:
Regarding the EU's international role, the Commission requests the Council and the European Parliament to confirm the Union's existing role as a participant, co-ordinator and, where necessary, negotiator in this area. 

The Communication also addresses a number of European policy issues that require further attention during the months to come, that will also require the continued support and cooperation of the Council and the Member States if the Commission's objectives are to be achieved. These including the Internet Domain Name System, IP rights, national country code top level domains, Alternative Dispute Reosultion, and Competition Policy.

In regards to data protection, "The Commission will continue discussions with ICANN and the US Government regarding data protection and privacy issues and the way these are reflected in the contractual framework between ICANN and the domain name Registries and Registrars. The Commission will also consider the ways in which data protection rules should be applied by the national ccTLD Registries in the Member States. The Commission may also recommend that ICANN and GAC adopt policies limiting the collection, processing and use of personal registration data, should that prove to be necessary."

In regard to competition policy, "the Commission confirms that the development of the Internet infrastructure is of critical importance for the economy of the European Union. The Commission wishes to reinforce the conclusions of the Lisbon European Council and to confirm that it is essential for the Member States to act as expeditiously as possible to implement the Commission's recommendations on leased line pricing and un-bundling of the local loop. That should accelerate affordable Internet access and use throughout European society and economy."

The Commission also informed the Council and the Parliament of the need to take additional actions to ensure and encourge full European participation in these developments, including: the new registry system must be implemented in a correct and timely way, including acceptable rules for data protection, competition and the identification and traceability of commercial operations2 and the appropriate protection of existing intellectual property rights.



The Commission also informed the Council and the Parliament of its intent to, among other steps, monitor the developments in ICANN and its constituent bodies, and the policies developed, since the allocation of these addresses will have a direct effect on the feasibility and the economics of routing, and therefore on the efficiency of the Internet environment; encourage the timely transition to IPv6, particularly within the European institutions and the public administrations in the Member States; facilitate the global expansion of the Internet, particularly in developing countries, through the transition from IPv4 to IPv6 addressing systems;

The Commission also notes of the European Union has a long-standing interest in the standardisation aspects of the information technologies from the point of view of interoperability and fair competition. As these technologies evolve globally, notably in the context of the Internet, the Commission intends to: • Continue to encourage European industrial and technical support and participation in the Orotocol Supporting Organisation (PSO) and its constituent bodies; Support international cooperation between the standardisation bodies comprising the PSO; • encourage within Europe increased awareness and use of the protocols being developed; • encourage enhanced involvement in the protocol development process by the organisations participating in related EU research projects; ensure that the existing neutrality of Internet specifications between alternative operating systems and other platforms is maintained and enhanced, particularly in view of the growing interest on the part of users in Open Software.

In regard to IPR in and around trademark-r domain names, "the Commission will continue to maintain a dialogue notably with WIPO and the US authorities on dispute resolution and the implementation of truly international alternative dispute resolution mechanisms. ... In view of the specific issues arising from domain name disputes, the Commission intends to make a proposal for a code of conduct or other appropriate instrument that would restrict the scope of current abuses in this area. This would include the identification of the categories of names to be protected and the treatment of trademarks and other recognised marks. The Commission will seek the cooperation of the Member States in the implementation of such a code of conduct, to be applied in the first instance to all TLD Registries operating in the European Union. The Commission will also take the necessary steps to ensure that similar disciplines are applied with equivalent effect by TLD Registries elsewhere, including the existing gTLDs."
column17:
The Communication emphasizes the European private sector's contribution to establishing the EU position at all levels of coordinating internet infrastructure, as well as membership and participation in ICANN as a precondition for the EU's successful participation from both user community and public policy viewpoints. Without that commitment, the public policy role of the EU and the Member States would be much less effective.

In the Communication, the EU also reports on the progress made in the United States and internationally, in transferring a number of functions relating to the organization and management of the Internet to the private sector. This process has involved transferring functions previously undertaken by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) under contract with the US Government to a new private organisation, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) and the merging of the IANA functions within ICANN.  

The Commission then detailed on pages 2- on the establishment of ICANN in 1998 and the responsibilities it is about to take from 2000.

The Commission notes the GAC' recommendation to ICANN stating that: “Country code top level domains are operated in trust by the Registry for the public interest, including the interest of the Internet community, on behalf of the relevant public authorities including governments, who ultimately have public policy over their ccTLDs, consistent with universal connectivity of the Internet.”
As such the Commission notes that in "view of the consensus that has been reached among the Member States and internationally, the Commission encourages the Member States to implement the GAC recommendations in an appropriate manner insofar as they relate to governments' relationships with ICANN and with their national ccTLD Registries. It would also be appropriate for the national ccTLD Registries in the European Union to adapt their policies and practices to achieve a high level of transparency in their operations. In so far as the national Registries accept registrations from entities and individuals from outside their territory, their dispute resolution policies should take full account of the interests of third parties in other Member States, and elsewhere. The Member States should also participate actively with their Registry organisations in the review of the registration policies and practices of the national ccTLDs and encourage the Registries to develop and implement registration policies consistent with the principles of the Internal Market and Competition policy. Meanwhile the Commission will continue to review whether the registration policies of the national ccTLD Registries are entirely consistent with EU internal market and competition law."

column4: Next Steps in Radio Spectrum Policy: Results of the Public Consultation on the Green Paper
Communication on the results of the public consultation on the 1999 communications review and orientations for the new regulatory framework
column16:
Key points from the summary by the Commission:
The Commission recognizes that the liberalisation of Europe's telecommunications market reached its peak on 1 January 1998 with the complete liberalisation of all telecommunications networks and services in virtually all Member States. Therefore, the Commission argued that this full liberalisation of Europe's telecommunications market by 1998, together with technological convergence across telecommunications, broadcasting, and information technology, rendered sector-specific regulation increasingly inadequate. In response, it proposed a more coherent and horizontal regulatory framework for communications infrastructure and services to support the transition to the Information Society.

It recognized the five principles should shape and govern European regulatory action going forward: having clearly defined objectives, being the minimum to meet these objectives, enhancing legal certainty, being technology neutral, and being enforced as closely as possible to the activities being regulated.

The regulatory framework will be structured around a a Framework Directive identifying general and specific policy objectives, and four specific directives on licensing, access and interconnection, universal service, privacy and data protection. Additionally, competition rules: greater reliance on the general competition rules of the Treaty, allowing much of the sectoral regulation to be replaced as competition becomes effective. Lastly,  accompanying non-binding measures such as recommendations, guidelines, and codes of conduct to  create a framework which can respond flexibly to changing market circumstances.

The Framework Directive will identify specific objectives for the Member States, guarantee specific consumer rights (for example dispute resolution procedures, emergency call numbers, increased transparency and access to information), ensure interoperability for communications services and equipment, set out the rights, responsibilities, decision making powers and procedures of regulatory authorites, and establish and lay down rules for the new designated committee. The Framework Directive will be accompanied by four specific directives based on Article 95 of the Treaty:

Directive on authorisations and licensing (including rules for the effective management of, and access to, scarce resources),
Directive on the provision of universal service, incorporating elements of the current Voice Telephony Directive and Interconnection Directive,
Directive on access and interconnection (based on the current Interconnection Directive and the TV Standards Directive),
Directive on data processing and protection of privacy in the electronic communications sector (directive updated and clarified to take account of technological developments.
Competition Law will become increasingly important in this sector and replace much of the sectoral regulation once competition becomes established on the market.

Specific policy goals:
* Internet -  The new framework would continue to treat Internet transmission services in the same way as other transmission services
* Licences and authorisations - using general authorisations as the basis for licensing communication networks and services, with specific authorisations reserved for the assignment of radio spectrum and numbers, ensuring that the fees for authorisations cover only justifiable and relevant administrative costs,
continuing to authorise the communications services provided via the Internet in an equivalent manner to other communications services (i.e. no specific regulation for the Internet).
Access and interconnection
Management of radio spectrum
Universal service
The interests of users and consumers - The current regulatory framework contains a number of provisions which aim to protect the interests of users and consumers in general. There are also a number of horizontal consumer protection directives at European level which apply to all sectors, including telecommunications. In this sector, the Commission proposes, among other, updating and clarifying the Telecoms Data Protection Directive to take account of technological developments and maintaining and consolidating existing obligations with regard to complaint handling and dispute settlement procedures.

At the EU level -  The Commission is not persuaded that a regulatory body at Community level would currently add sufficient value to justify the likely costs. The Commission therefore does not propose to” establish a European Regulatory Authority for communications services at this stage.  But co-operation between the Commission and national regulators must urgently be improved.  Where necessary, solutions agreed in the designated High Level Communications Group of National Regulatory Authorities and the Commission  would be backed up by legal measures adopted by the Commission under its executive powers, with the assistance of a new Communications Committee.

Later, the Commission the result of its consulation with stakeholders: The consultation revealed broad support for maintaining sector-specific regulation alongside competition law, adopting a technology-neutral framework covering all communications infrastructure, strengthening harmonisation, expanding general authorisations, promoting efficient spectrum management, preserving universal service and standardisation, and ensuring strong independent national regulators. The Commission also identified areas of disagreement, including spectrum allocation, significant market power, universal service affordability, and institutional arrangements, before proposing a new regulatory framework comprising a Framework Directive and four specific Directives.

Key points from the communication:
*  Since 1990, the European Commission has progressively put in place a comprehensive regulatory framework for the liberalisation of the telecommunications market.

*  An advanced communications industry is a pre-condition of Europe’s transition to the Information Society.

*  Without efficient, high quality communications, European industry, and in particular small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), face a major disadvantage in relation to their global competitors.

*  Telecommunications liberalisation will continue to have a major impact on the economy as a whole.

*  This Communication presents the main elements of the Commissions policy proposals for a new regulatory framework, to cover all communications infrastructure and associated services. [...]  With these proposals, the Commission seeks to build on the successes of the current regime and ensure that regulation at EU level continues to encourage the development of a competitive single European market.

* while the Communication recognizes several trends that shape the market, it recognizes in particular the development of digital television.

*  The existing legislative framework was primarily designed to manage the transition to competition and was therefore focused on the creation of a competitive market and the rights of new entrants. The new policy framework will seek to reinforce competition in all market segments, particularly at local level. It should be designed to cater for new, dynamic and largely unpredictable markets with many more players than today.

Three policy objectives: 1)  To promote and sustain an open and competitive European market for communications services, 2) To benefit the European citizen; and 3)  To consolidate the internal market in a converging environment  by removing obstacles to the provision of communications networks and services

column4: The Commission communication "Principles and guidelines for the Community's audio-visual policy in the digital age", and the Council conclusions of 6 June 2000 welcoming this communication.
column16:
Main takeaway: The Communications informed operators and interested parties of the Commission's audiovisual startegy to address the changes brought by digital technologies. Alongside the benefits of new forms of content and creation of high-skilled jobs, the Commission want to safeguard certain public interests that may be jeopredise due to important content. Particularly, the Commission sought to protect cultural and linguistic diversity, minor and consumer protection. The content should be regulated according to its nature, and not according to its means of delivery.  Adoption should be evolutionary not revolutionary. The Commission considers that a balanced approach to public service broadcasting is needed and self-regulatory mechanisms may well play a bigger role in achieving public interest objectives.

Additional points:
"Digitisation means not only a quantum leap in the amount of audiovisual content and information available to the citizen, but allows a wide range of new operators to participate in the production and distribution of audiovisual content and information world-wide. For the audiovisual sector major changes are already underway: it is possible that within a decade, analogue broadcasting will have been phased out in many Member States and replaced entirely by digital broadcasting."

"Secondly, the Community must maximise the competitivity of the European audiovisual industry in order to ensure that digitisation does not simply result in a flood of imported or archive (repeated) material. The European audiovisual industry must remain capable of providing quality audiovisual content that is of relevance and importance to European citizens"

"In this context, one must recall the simple fact that the European audiovisual market remains overwhelmingly dominated by American productions. The annual EU trade deficit with the USA in this sector is approaching 7 billion Euro6. American productions account for between 60 and 90% of Member States' audiovisual markets (receipts from cinema ticket sales, video cassette sales and rentals and from sales of television fiction programmes), whilst the respective European share of the American market is of the order of 1 or 2%"

"The audiovisual media play a central role in the functioning of modern democratic societies. Without the free flow of information; such societies cannot function. Moreover, the audiovisual media play a fundamental role in the development and transmission of social values. This is not simply because they influence to a large degree which facts about and which images of the world we encounter, but also because they provide concepts and categories- political, social, ethnic, geographical, psychological and so on- which we use to render these facts and images intelligible. They therefore help to determine not only what we see of the world but also how we see it. The audiovisual industry is therefore not an industry like any other and does not simply produce goods to be sold on the market like other goods. It is in fact a cultural industry par excellence. It has a major influence on what citizens know, believe and feel and plays a crucial role in the transmission, development and even construction of cultural identities. This is true above all with regard to children."

"It is for these reasons that the broadcasting sector, one of the main vectors of audiovisual content, has, since its inception, been subject to specific regulation in the general interest. [...] All Member States have imposed public service obligations, which are implemented in particular by public service broadcasters. Regulation of the sector is increasingly carried out by bodies or institutions independent of government. Furthermore, Member States have implemented financial and other support instruments intended to promote the creation, production and distribution of audiovisual works. The audiovisual policy of the European Community has incorporated these principles and common objectives and developed its own instruments according to its particular competence, notably as regards the freedom to provide services and support for the industry. At the regulatory level, the "Television without Frontiers" Directive9 established a legal framework ensuring the freedom to provide television broadcasting services in the Community, taking due account of certain well defined general interests (in particular: the protection of minors, the promotion of cultural diversity and consumer protection). As regards support measures at European level, the Media I and Media II programmes complemented and built on actions by Member States by supporting training, project development and the distribution of European works. Finally, the Community has always attached great importance to promoting technological innovation in the audiovisual sector, for example through Directive 95/47/EC on the use of standards for the transmission of television signals10, which aimed to establish an appropriate regulatory regime for the start-up phase of new digital television services. Equally, the Action Plan for the promotion of Wide Screen (16/9) Television11, contributed to the take-off of this market and there were specific actions on new technologies in the Media I and Media II programmes"

The Commission seeks to keep protecting the fundamental goals of the European policy, namely to encourage the production and distribution of European works, by establishing legal framework to guarantee the freedom to provide audiovisual services, but at the same time taking account of how to mobilse not just traditional market players (radio, cinema, and television) but also new players brought by the digital resoultion, for example, producers of new forms of audiovisual content (p. 8-9).

The Commission's principles for regulatory intervention:
1. The principle of proportionality, which dictates that the degree of regulatory intervention should not be more than is necessary to achieve the objective in question. The principle is exemplified by the Television without frontiers directive, the IPR directives, and the upcoming Directive on electronic commerce.
2. Seperation of transport and content regulation - the Commission identifies a consensus that on the need for separate approaches to the regulation of the transport of electronic signals and the infrastructure used for this on the one hand, and the regulation of content including audiovisual content on the other. [..,] In applying the distinction between transport and content, particular attention must be paid to questions relating to consumers' access to content, for example with regard to EPGs and “must carry” rules.
3. General interest objectives and the regulatory approach at the European level - "The Commission considers that the digital revolution does not call into question the need for audiovisual policy to identify relevant general interests and, where necessary, to protect them through the regulatory process. Technological developments, however, call for ongoing evaluation of the means and methods used, in order to ensure that they continue to be proportionate to the objectives to be achieved. [...] Agraduated approach to regulation will be required to deal with the general interests affected by each type of service. The basic rationale for this regulation should be the failure of the market, real or potential, to reach these objectives (except in certain cases, such as the protection of minors or copyright, where market forces are not adapted to the achievement of such objectives). It should take into account the commercial or non-commercial nature of the transactions involved and the degree of control and choice which can be exercised by the users."
4. Recognition of the role of public service broadcasting and the need for transparency in its financing - The future of the dual system of broadcasting in Europe, comprising public and private broadcasters, depends on the role of public service broadcasters being reconciled with the principles of fair competition and the operation of a free market. Member States are free to confer and define their public service remit and how to finance public service broadcasters, but this funding scheme must respect the principle of proporionality, not affect trading conditions, with the Commission having the duty to ensure that the funding scheme is compatible with the treaty, ECJ case law, and in respect of both state aid rules and the freedom to provide services.
5.Self-regulation: a complementary process - operators and users can contribute to the achievement of the public interests set by governments and public authorities through the development of self-regulatory measures, obviating the need for detailed regulation. The development of codes of conduct at the EU level should be encourage. Self-regulation is more desirable in some sectors, but not others (such as copyrights). Self-regulation should also not be a way for major incumbent operators to define the rules of the game.
6. Regulatory authorities should be independent; in line with the principle of subsidiarity, therefore, content regulation is primarily the responsibility of Member States. Regulators accros sectors should co-operate (communication infrastrcture, audiovisual sector, and competition). Regulators should contribute to the development and implementation of self-regulation, with the Commission examining the establishment of a a specific forum for European-level co-operation between regulators, operators and consumers in the audiovisual sector.

Steps to be taken:
1. Review the Television without frontier directive.
2. In regard to the issue of access to audiovisual content, while the Commissionrecognizses the importance of acces to audiovisual content, given the early stage when market and technological developments are highly unpredictable, the Commission does not propose any specific action for the audio-visual sector, but notes that this is an area to be monitored closely. 
3. The Commission considers the rapid adoption of the proposed Directive on Copyright and Related Rights in the Information Society to be of paramount importance.
4. The Commission plans to present an evaluative report regarding the protection of minors as well as carry out a study into new advertising techniques in view of a possible future evaluation of the provisions contained in the Television without Frontiers Directive.
5. It plans to present a communication legal aspects relating to the cinema sector

Lastly, the Commission recognizes the Community’s audiovisual policy has two central external dimensions: The enlargement of the European Union offers many opportunities for the European audiovisual industry and, more generally, for cultural and linguistic diversity in Europe. Second, while audiovisual services are covered by GATS, the Community and the Member States made no commitment under it so they therefore maintained their freedom of action regard to both existing and future measures at national and Community level. The Commission also recognises that given the trend towards globalisation, there is an increasing need for the Community to develop its dialogue both with industry and with consumers at the international level.

column4: Council resolution of 3 October 2000 on the organisation and management of the Internet
column16:
The Council issued a resolution regarding the organization and management of the Internet. In it, it recalls a joint EU-US statement on electronic commerce that the particular role of the state as to provide "a consistent and predictable legal framework, …and to ensure adequate protection of public interest objectives such as privacy,
intellectual property rights, prevention of fraud, consumer protection and public safety"; 

It also emphasized that the greater consideration for public policies and the pursuit of globalization of the
Management of Internet addresses and domain names are key objectives for the European
Union. It also recognized the importance of the development of electronic commerce, which will require efficient and transparent management of the resources represented by domain names and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, in particular through the deployment of the next generation of addresses using the IPv6 standard.

The Council also recognized the important involvement of the Member States, the Commission, and internet professionals (including from the private sector) in setting up ICANN.

It notes that number of issues were still not resolved, inlcuding the nature of, and arrangements for, balanced and equal oversight of some of ICANN's activities by public authorities, the rules to govern generic domains, the redelegation of certain ccTLDs to another manager at the request of the Government concerned, and the transfer of the management of the root server system from the US Department of Commerce to ICANN, under appropriate international supervision by public authorities.

For the Council, these issues had to be addressed with due regard for both the interests of the international community as a whole and the public policy challenges involved, particularly as regards competition, personal data protection and respect for intellectual property rights.

It also called the Member States to consult each other with a view to establishing common European positions on the subject in the international bodies concerned and to securing genuine globalization of Internet management, to take due account of the policy objectives listed by the Commission communication, and to implement, in accordance with national provisions, the principles adopted by the GAC on domain name management.

It resoulved to instruct the Commission to encourage the coordination of policies on Internet management, in particular by defining an appropriate framework to organise and structure activities in this area, o continue its efforts, in consultation with the Member States, to achieve genuine globalisation of Internet management with due regard for the imperatives of both public policies and international agreements, to set up a European network bringing together the scientific, technical and legal skills that currently exist in the Member States with regard to domain name, address and Internet protocol management.

The regulation seeks to regulate the internal market by ensuring free movement of information society services. 

It requires member states to ensure that information society services comply with laws in the coordinated sector/field. They must ensure that taking up or pursuiting an activity of an information society service provider may not be made subject to prior authorisation or any other requirement having equivalent effect. Regulated entities must provide at least the information described in Articles 5-7.
It also prohibits member states from imposing a general obligation on providers to monitor the information which  they transmit or store, nor a general obligation actively to seek facts or circumstances indicating illegal activity, but they may require providers to promptly inform the authorities of alleged illegal activities or require them to provide information enabling the identification of recipients of their service with whom they have storage agreements.
Member states must also ensure that court actions allow for the rapid adoption of measures designed to terminate any alleged infringement.

Member states must also ensure adequate means of supervision and investigation necessary to implement the directive effectively as well as receive information from regulated entities. They must also cooperate with other member states and provide them with information and assistance.  
Member states also determine the sanctions applicable to infridgement of national provisions and shall take necessary measures to ensure they are enforced. Sanctions must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive.

It also receives information on significant decisions by bodies responsible for out-of-court dispute settlement as well as from member states regarding significant administrative or judicial decisions. It may particularly analyse the need for proposals concerning the liability of providers of hyperlinks and location tool services, "notice and take down" procedures and the attribution of liability following the taking down of content. t. The directive sets a self-regulatory regime with prescriptive rules on information provision and a conditional liability regime within regulated entities operate. Providers that are mere conduits can transmit communications without liability as long as they do not initiate the transmission, select the recievers of the transmission, or select or modify the information contain in it. They can store the information for the purpose of transfering the information and not longer than necessary. Providers that are caching services can temporary store information for the sole purpose of making more efficient the information's onward transmission without liability as long as the do not modify the information, complies with the conditions on accessing the information, complies with rules regarding the update of information based on rules widely  recognized and used by the industry, the do not intefer with the lawful use of technology widely recognised and used by industry, to obtain data on the use of the information; and acts expeditionally to remove or to disable access to the information it has stored upon obtaining actual knowledge of the fact that the information at the initial source of the transmission has been removed from the network, or access to it has been disabled, or that a court or an administrative authority has ordered such removal or disablement.
Providers of hosting services are not liabile as long as they do not have actual knowledge of illegal activities or information or are not aware of facts or circumstances from which the illegal activity or information is apparent; and when obtain such knoweldge or awareness acts expeditiously to remove or to disable access to the information.

Providers have no general obligations to monitor information the transmit or store, nor a general obligation actively to seek facts or circumstances indicating illegal activity.

The directives prescribe which information must at least be provided clearly, comprehensibly and unambiguously and prior to the service being placed in the market. 

The regulations rely on professional associations and bodies to establish codes of conduct to determine the types of information that can be given for the purposes of commercial communication; the Commission then needs to take account of these codes when drawing up proposals for community initiatives. 
Regulated service providers can also indicate any relevant codes they are subscribed to and information on how those codes can be consulted electronically. 

The Member States and the Commission can both encourage the drawing up of codes of conduct from trade, professional and consumer associations or organisations, designed to contribute to the proper implementation of Articles 5 to 15 (the latter of which address the no general monitoring obligation), including transmitting codes to the Commission and making these codes accessible electronically. Codes may also be drawn to protect minors and human dignity. The Commission and the member states shall encourage the involvement of associations or organisations representing consumers in the drafting and implementation of codes of conduct affecting their interests, as well associations representing the visually impaired and disabled.

Member states are permitted to maintain or introduce measures in conformity with Community law which contain more detailed provisions than those set out in this Regulation. They, through their designated regulatory authority must ensure harging for unbundled access to the local loop fosters fair and sustainable competition. The authorities can impose changes on the reference offer for unbundled access and require opearators to supply information relevant for the implementation of this regulation. Beneficiaries should not have to pay for  network elements or facilities which are not necessary for the supply of its services. They must meet reasonable requests from beneficiaries for unbundled access to their local loops and related facilities, under transparent, fair and non-discriminatory conditions. They can only refuse based on objective criteria, relating to technical feasibility or the need to maintain network integrity. They shall also shall provide beneficiaries with facilities equivalent to those provided for their own services or to their associated companies, and with the same conditions and time-scales.

The Directive is a right-awarding regime that requires the Member States to provide exclusive rights to authorize or prohibit direct or indirect, temporary or permanent reproduction by any means and in any form. It also requires the awarding of a right of communication to the public of works and right of making available to the public other subject-matter and a distribution right.

Member States may establish limited exceptions to copyright reproduction, communication, and distribution rights for purposes such as private use, education, research, accessibility, journalism, public interest, libraries, parody, and other specified non-commercial or socially beneficial uses, provided they do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of rightholders.

Member States must also provide adequate legal protection against circumvention of any effective technological measures, which the person concerned carries out in the knowledge, or with reasonable grounds to know, that he or she is pursuing that objective. Member States must also prohibit the manufacture, distribution, marketing, commercial possession, or provision of devices and services designed or primarily used to circumvent technological protection measures. The Directive also defines effective technological protection measures and requires Member States to ensure that they do not prevent beneficiaries from exercising statutory copyright exceptions and limitations where applicable.

Member States must also provide legal protection for electronic rights-management information by prohibiting its unauthorized removal, alteration, and use in ways that facilitate copyright infringement.

column4: Regulation on Personal Data Processed by EU Institutions (predecessor)
column16:
The aim of the regulation is to regulate how European Institutions protect fundamental rights and freedoms, particularly the right to privacy with respect to the processing of personal data. It also establishes the European Data Protection Supervisor to monitor the application of the regulation.
The EDPS can offer prior checking for processes that present specific risks and offer consultation to Community institutions and the Commission.

It requires EU institutions to process personal data fairly and lawfully, and to collect it for specific, explicit and legitimate purposes; be adequate, relevant and not excessive; be accurate and kept up to date; and be kept in a form which permits identification for no longer than necessary. The regulation also sets criteria for making data processing legitimate and changing the purpose of the processing, as well as for transferring data between institutions. It also defines how to process special categories of data and what information should be given to data subjects.

The Regulation then assigns data subject rights against the institutions.

Institutions processing personal data must maintain confidentiality and security. They also had to maintain privacy in the context of the use and operation of telecommunications networks or terminal equipment. 

The regulation also defines the relationshis between EU institutions, EDPS, the Commission and the Member States.

The Regulation also establishes the EDPS as a regulatory authority monitoring and ensuring the proper application of the Regulation. The Supervisor has term limitations, work independently, expertise, secrecy,  and the Parliament, Council and Commission determine its regulations, general conditions, budget, and duties. 

The EDPS monitors compliance, investigates complaints, advises EU institutions, conducts inspections, cooperates with other supervisory authorities, and exercises corrective and enforcement powers, including ordering compliance and banning unlawful processing.
