The aim of the directive is to harmonize the provisions regarding the processing of personal data in electronic communications. It particularise and complement Directive 95/46/EC.

Member States may set exceptions regarding transparent procedures governing the way in which a provider of a public communications network and/or a publicly available electronic communications service may override 1) the elimination of the presentation of calling line identification and 2) the elimination of the presentation of calling line identification and the temporary denial or absence of consent of a subscriber or user for the processing of location data.


Member States must also ensure that subscribers are informed, free of charge and before they are included in the directory, about the purpose(s) of a printed or electronic directory of subscribers available to the public or obtainable through directory enquiry services, in which their personal data can be included and of any further usage possibilities based on search functions embedded in electronic versions of the directory. Subscribers should be able to determine whether their personal data is included in a public directory and, if so, to verify, correct or withdraw such data.

The Directive also regulates Member States, ensuring they do not place any mandatory requirements for specific technical features on terminals or other electronic communication equipment that could impede the placing of equipment on the market and the free circulation of such equipment in and between Member States. They must inform the Commission in accordance with Directive 98/34.
They may adopt measures to ensure that terminal equipment is designed to respect users' rights to safeguard and control their personal data, in line with Directive 1999/5/EC and Council Decision 87/95/EEC from 22 December 1986 concerning standardisation in information technology and communications (The R&TTE Directive).

They may restrict the scope of rights and obligations under specific articles when such restriction constitutes a necessary, appropriate and proportionate measure within a democratic society to safeguard national security (i.e. State security), defence, public security, and the prevention, investigation, detection and prosecution of criminal offences or of unauthorised use of the electronic communication system.

The Commission is tasked with reviewing the Directive, and it may request information from the Member States, which shall be supplied without undue delay
column17:
The Directive sets a self-regulatory regime based on prescriptive, process-based regulation.
Providers must take appropriate technical and organizational measures to safeguard the security of their services; they must inform their subscribers in cases of breach, risks, and potential remedies.
Providers must also ensure the confidentiality of communications and prohibit listening or tapping.
They must erase or anonymize data relating to subscribers and users when it is no longer necessary. The Directive also sets rules regarding the processing of location data other than traffic data. 

Providers must also offer users the possibility, using a simple means and free of charge, of preventing the presentation of the calling line identification on a per-call basis.pquirements.

The Directive also regulates automated calling systems, fax, or email for direct marketing so they can only be used with prior subscriber consent.

column16:
Within the framework set by the Framework Directive, this Directive regulates how Member States regulate access to and interconnection of electronic communications networks and associated facilities. In accordance with internal market principles, it aims to establish a regulatory framework for the relationships between suppliers of networks and services that will result in sustainable competition, interoperability of electronic communications services, and consumer benefits. The regulation does so by establishing rights and obligations for operators and enterprises and by setting out objectives for regulatory authorities. Among others, it deals with the regulation of wide-screen television services.

The national authorities need to operate to pursue the objectives set ion the Framework Directive and encourage adequate access and interconnection, and interoperability of services. They should efficiency, sustainable competition, and gives the maximum benefit to end-users.

They may impose in a objective, transparent, proportionate and non-discriminatory: 1) obligations on undertakings that control access to end-users, including the obligation to interconnect their networks; 2) obligations on operators to provide access on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms to ensure accessibility for end-users to digital radio and television broadcasting services; 3) lay down technical or operational conditions to be met by the provider and/or beneficiaries to ensure normal operation of the network; 4). Regulatory authorities may intervene, on request or at their own initiative, where justified to secure the policy objectives of the Framework Directive.

Member States must ensure that the conditions laid down in Annex I, Part I apply. Regulatory authorities need to conduct a periodic market analysis review of the conditions set in Annex I, Part I. The regulatory authority is particularly allowed to amend or withdraw conditions if it finds after the market analysis that an operator does not (or no longer) have significant market power, to the extent that it does not adversely affect end-users' accessibility and do not adversely affect the prospect for effective competition in the markets for retail digital television and radio broadcasting services, conditional access systems, and other facilities. After the market analysis, the regulatory authorities may also decide to maintain, amend, or withdraw obligations set by earlier Directives, such as 97/33, 98/10, and 92/44. They shall impose obligations where they identify operators with significant market power. In cases where an authority decides to impose obligations not set out in the Directive on operators with significant market power, it should inform the Commission and request its approval to do so. 

Annex I requires Member States to ensure that conditional access systems for digital television and radio operate on fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory terms, promote interoperability through open licensing and common interfaces, maintain separate accounts for access services, and, where appropriate, provide access to essential facilities such as application programming interfaces (APIs) and electronic programme guides (EPGs).
Member States may also impose transparency obligations requiring operators to make public specified information, such as accounting information, technical specifications, network characteristics, terms and conditions for supply and use, and prices. It may also place an obligation of non-discrimination requiring opeators to publish  a reference offer, which shall be sufficiently unbundled to ensure that undertakings are not required to pay for facilities which are not necessary for the service requested, giving a description of the relevant offerings broken down into components according to market needs, and the associated terms and conditions including prices. 

The regulatory authority may also impose obligations of non-discrimination, obligations for accounting separation in relation to specific activities, obligations relating to price control or cost accounting, or obligations of access to, or use of, specific network facilities. The regulatory authority must publish these obligations.

The Member States must inform the Commission of the identity of national authorities that are responsible for the tasks set by the Directive, and they, in turn, inform the Commission of the identity of operators with significant market power and the obligations placed on them (including any changes). The Member States must also inform the Commission on the laws, regulation, and administrative provisions implementing the Directive. The Commission reviews the functioning of this Directive.

Annex I may be amended in light of market and technical developments.
The Commission is assisted by a Committee established under the Framework Directive.
column17:
Self-regulation is operationalized under the shadow of the obligations that regulatory authorities may place on providers as permitted by the Directive and its Annex I, particularly those with significant market power. The Directive establishes a regulatory regime that requires Member States not to impose restrictions preventing undertakings, whether within one Member State or across different Member States, from negotiating agreements among themselves on technical and commercial arrangements for access and/or interconnection. Similarly, it prevents Member States from requiring authorization from enterprises that seek interconnection but do not provide services or operate a network in that Member State. Member States also cannot adopt measures that oblige operators to offer different terms and conditions to different undertakings for equivalent services and/or impose obligations unrelated to the actual access and interconnection services provided, without prejudice to the conditions set out in the Authorization Directive.

The Directive also sets both a right and an obligation for regulated operators to negotiate interconnection with each other for the purpose of providing publicly available electronic communications services, in order to ensure the provision and interoperability of services throughout the Community. They must offer terms and conditions consistent with the obligations imposed by the national authorities.

The Directive also sets two specific requirements. First, that public electronic communications networks established for the distribution of digital television services shall be capable of distributing wide-screen television services and programs. The aim of this Directive is to ensure that the freedom to provide electronic communications networks and services is subject only to the conditions laid down in this Directive and to any restrictions in conformity with Article 46(1) of the Treaty, in particular measures regarding public policy, public security and public health. It aims to implement an internal market in electronic communications networks and services through the harmonisation and simplification of authorisation rules and conditions in order to facilitate their provision throughout the Community.

Same as before, the Directive mostly allows member states to subject the provision of electronic communications services to general obligations, meaning undertaking may need to notify but are not required to obtain an explicit decision. Unlike before, there is no longer option for specific licenses.
A general authorisation may provide specific rights, including electronic communications services, negotiate interconnection with and where applicable obtain access to or interconnection from other providers of publicly available communications networks (from anywhere in the Community),  be given an opportunity to be designated to provide different elements of a universal service and/or to cover different parts of the national territory in accordance with the Universal Service Directive (Directive 2002/22/EC).

The Member States may place in the general authorizationsuthorisations only conditions listed in the Annex. These conditions must be objectively justified, non-discriminatory, proportionate and tThese obligations shall be legally separated from the obligations set on providers of electronic communications networks and services by ether the Access or Universal Service Directives.

The Annex requires Member States to ensure that conditional access systems for digital television and radio operate on fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory terms, promote interoperability through open licensing and common interfaces, maintain separate accounts for access services, and, where appropriate, provide access to essential facilities such as application programming interfaces (APIs) and electronic programme guides (EPGs).

The Member States are also constraint in regarding to limiting the number of rights of use around granting radio frequencies.  Before they can do that , they must give due weight to the need to maximise benefits for users and to facilitate the development of competition, give all interested parties the ability to express their views, publish any decision and the its reasoning, invite applications for rights of use (After determining the relevant procedures) and  review the limitation at reasonable intervals or at the reasonable request.

Haronization and standardisation requirements (although not by harmonising standards) also limit member states' discretion: 1) Member States shall grant the right to use radio frequencies where their usage is harmonised, access conditions are agreed, procedures are in place, and frequencies are assigned based on international and Community rules. 2) At a firm's request, authorities must issue declarations within one week, confirming if the firm submitted a notification under Article 3(2) and detailing when providers of electronic communications networks or services can apply for rights to install, negotiate interconnection, or access to support those rights with other government levels or firms.

Member States may require regulated entities to provide information necessary to verify compliance with the conditions of the general authorization or of rights of use or with the specific obligations. In cases of non-compliance, regulated entities have a reaonable opportunity and time to state its view or remedey any breach. It may take appropriate measures if the breaches are not remedied, including imposing financial penalties or prevent the regulated entity from providing electronic communications networks or services or suspend or withdraw rights of use.
Overall, regulatory authorities may request information under general authorisation, for rights of use, or the specific oblgiations that is proportionate and objectively justify, and for: 1) verifying compliance, 2) granting or assessing rights of use, 3) publication of comparative overviews of quality and price of services, 4) clearly defined statistical purposes, 5) market analysis under the Access Directive or the Universal Service Directive.

The Directive also limits the ability of the regulatory authorities to impose administrative fines on undertakings. In total, it may only the administrative costs which will be incurred in the management, control and enforcement of the general authorisation scheme and of rights of use and of specific obligations. In addition, it may include costs of  international cooperation, harmonisation and standardisation, market analysis, monitoring compliance and other market control, as well as regulatory work involving preparation and enforcement of secondary legislation and administrative decisions. Any charge must be objective, transparent and proportionate manner which minimises additional administrative costs and attendant charges. Member States may also permit the regulatory authorities to impose fees for the figts of use and  ensure that such fees shall be objectively justified, transparent, non-discriminatory and proportionate in relation to their intended purpose.

The Member States are also only permitted to amend the terms of the general authorisations and rights of use or rights to install facilities may only be amended in objectively justified cases and in a proportionate manner. They have to give notice; they must publish all relevant information on rights, conditions, procedures, charges, fees and decisions concerning general authorisations and rights of use is published.

There is a transition period for prior authorizations, which may be extended until at the latest nine months. The Member States must notify the Commission in such situations.They may prove that the abolition of an authorisation condition regarding access to electronic communications networks, which was in force before the date of entry into force of this Directive, creates excessive difficulties for undertakings, but must request a temporary prolongation from the Commission. The Commission shall consider such a request, taking into account the particular situation in that Member State and of the undertaking(s) concerned, and the need to ensure a coherent regulatory environment at a Community level. 

The Commission is taked with the responsibility to review the national authorisation systems.

column16:
The Directive establishes a regulatory framework harmonizing by way of laying down tasks and procedures for the regulation of electronic communications services, electronic communications networks, associated facilities, and associated services. 

The Directive requires Member States to ensure that regulatory authorities under this Directive and the other Specific Directives are competent and independent. Specifically, the directive completes the separation between regulators and service providers by requiring that regulated authorities be independent from all organisations providing electronic communications networks, equipment, or services. Member States that retain ownership or control of undertakings providing electronic communications networks and/or services shall ensure effective structural separation of the regulatory function from activities associated with ownership or control. It similarly, required the Member States to inform the Commission of the identity of the regulatory authorities assigned responsibilities under the Directives (including the specific Directive) and their respective responsibilities (as they are no longer have to be the telecommunication administrations).
Regulatory authorities must exercise their power impartially and transparently. 
Regulatory authorities should also, when appropriate, consult and cooperate with similar authorities and authorities entrusted with the implementation of competition law and consumer protection (again marking the two main mechanisms of neo-liberalism.

The member states must also ensure actors affected by decisions made by the regulatory authorities can appeal their decision to a body, which may be a court, that has appropriate expertise.

Regulatory authorities must provide information to the Commission so it could perform its tasks. Where the information provided refers to information previously provided by undertakings at the request of the national regulatory authority, such undertakings shall be informed thereof. To the extent necessary, and unless the authority that provides the information has made an explicit and reasoned request to the contrary, the Commission shall make the information provided available to another such authority in another Member State.

The Directive also requires that if a regulatory authority plans to take measures in accordance to this or any other Specific directive, it will give impacted parties opportunity to comment; they will also be transparent regarding their consultation procedures and its results. 

The Directive also requires the national authorities to take account of the objectives set in this Directive, contribute to the development of the internal market for electronic communications, and cooperate among themselves and the Commission to ensure consistent application of the Directive (the Commission seems to get a more critical role). They should, in particular, agree on instruments and remedies. The Directive establishes the objectives and guiding principles for national regulatory authorities in electronic communications. It requires regulators to adopt proportionate and technologically neutral measures that promote competition, support the EU internal market, and protect citizens through universal service, consumer rights, privacy, transparency, inclusion, and secure communications networks.

If authorities plan to take measures to achieve these objectives that would affect trade among member states, they have to share the draft and its reasoning with the Commission and the other regulatory authorities for their comments. If the measures would create a barrier, the Commission may take a decision to require the authority to withdraw its draft measure.

The Directive then defines for the specific when an undertaking have significant market power - if, either individually or jointly with others, it enjoys a position equivalent to dominance, that is to say a position of economic strength affording it the power to behave to an appreciable extent independently of competitors, customers and ultimately consumers. Where an undertaking has significant market power on a specific market, it may also be deemed to have significant market power on a closely related market, where the links between the two markets are such as to allow the market power held in one market to be leveraged into the other market. The Commission provide guidelines on market analysis and the assessment of significant market power. It may also, after public consultation and consultation with regulatory authorities adopt recommendations on relevant product and service markets within the elctronic communications sectors of which may be such as to justify the imposition of regulatory obligations set out in the Specific Directives, without prejudice to markets that may be defined in specific cases under competition law. The Commission shall define markets in accordance with the principles of competition law.
Regulatory authorities must take utmost account of the recommendations and guidelines when defining relevant market appropriate to national circumstances, in particular relevant geographic markets within their territory, in accordance with the principles of competition law. The procedure for market analysis is defined in the Directive, and it should be carried out, where appropriate, in collaboration with the national competition authorities. The market analysis can lead to a determination to impose, maintain, amend or withdraw obligations on undertakings, which may be withdrawn where the authority reaches a conclusion that the market is effectively competitive. If it finds that a market is not effectively competitive, it may identify undertakings with significant market power and impose obligations. 
The Commission may also identify tansnational markets, In such markets, several authorities conduct the market analysis and decide to gether on any imposition, maintenance, amendment or withdrawal of regulatory obligations.

The Commission ensures harmonisation in other ways. The Framework Directive establishes a hierarchy of standards to promote interoperability and harmonisation in electronic communications. The European Commission publishes and encourages the use of European standards, drawing on international standards by ITU/ISO/IEC where appropriate, especially when European standards are absent or reference to them is not published. If voluntary adoption proves insufficient to ensure interoperability, the Commission may make specific standards mandatory after public consultation, and may later revise or withdraw them if they become outdated, ineffective, or hinder technological development.
The Commission may also issues recommendations to Member States on the harmonised application of the provisions in this Directive and the Specific Directives in order to further the achievement of the objectives. Member States shall ensure that national regulatory authorities take the utmost account of those recommendations in carrying out their tasks. Where a national regulatory authority chooses not to follow a recommendation, it shall inform the Commission giving the reasoning for its position. Where the Commission finds that divergence at national level in regulations aimed at implementing Article 10(4) creates a barrier to the single market, the Commission may, acting in accordance with the procedure referred to in Article 22(3), take the appropriate technical implementing measures.

The Directive combines competitionompetititon and consumer protection law logic into the regulation of the telecommunication sector.

The directive concerns the provision of electrocnic communications networks and services to end-users, by ensuring availability throughout the Community of good quality publicly available services through effective competition and choice and to deal with circumstances in which the needs of end-users are not satisfactorily met by the market. The Directive establishes the rights of end-users and the corresponding obligations on undertakings providing publicly available electronic communications networks and services.

Chapter II of the Directive establishes universal service obligations. It establishes universal service obligations to ensure that all end users, regardless of location, have access to affordable, high quality basic telecommunications services, including telephone access, functional internet connectivity, directories, public payphones, emergency services, and measures for disabled users. It also allows Member States to designate one or more providers to deliver these services through objective, transparent, non-discriminatory, and cost-effective procedures while minimising market distortions. The remainder of the chapter establishes how universal service obligations should be implemented, monitored, financed, and updated. It requires regulators to ensure the affordability of services through tariff oversight and special pricing schemes where needed, enable users to control expenditure, monitor and enforce service quality, calculate and compensate the net costs of universal service where these impose an unfair burden on providers, ensure transparency in financing arrangements, and periodically review the scope of universal service to reflect social, economic, and technological developments.

Chapter III establishes an ex post competition regime for electronic communications markets. National regulatory authorities must periodically analyse retail markets and identify undertakings with significant market power (SMP). Where competition is ineffective, they may impose, maintain, amend, or withdraw proportionate obligations, including retail price controls, cost accounting, leased-line obligations, and carrier selection and pre-selection requirements, subject to Commission oversight and the Framework Directive's market review procedures. Same as under the Framework Directive, the Commission can identify transnational markets.

Chapter IV meanwhile establishes end-user rights and consumer protection obligations in electronic communications. It requires providers to ensure transparent contracts, pricing and service information, quality of service, network integrity, interoperability, directory and emergency services, number portability, and access to essential telecommunications facilities, while empowering national regulatory authorities to oversee compliance and impose proportionate obligations where necessary.

Lastly, Chapter V contains the Directive's implementation, consultation, and governance provisions. It allows Member States to make additional services beyond universal service publicly available free of charge, requires consultation with stakeholders on end-user and consumer-rights-related issues, promotes out-of-court dispute resolution, empowers the Commission to update technical annexes, and establishes procedures for notification, monitoring, committee oversight, and implementation. The designated committee set up by the Framework directive assist the Commission.
column17:
The Directive operationalises self-regulation under the assumption that competitive markets should regulate themselves. Under this premise, the EU constrains Member States' ability to intervene in telecommunications markets by conditioning intervention on a market-corrective regulatory model, whereby intervention occurs only upon demonstrated market failure. National regulatory authorities may impose obligations only after a prescribed market analysis demonstrates ineffective competition and identifies an undertaking with significant market power. Regulation therefore becomes contingent on evidence of market failure, allowing competitive markets to operate without ex ante intervention. Once effective competition is restored, those obligations must be withdrawn. 

Under its consumer protection logic, Chapter IV of the Directive operationalises process-based self-regulation by requiring providers to develop and implement their own contractual, organisational, and technical arrangements to meet statutory consumer protection and service-quality objectives, subject to regulatory oversight and intervention by national regulatory authorities.

Chapter V further operationalises self-regulation by encouraging interested parties, including consumers, user groups, and service providers, to develop and monitor voluntary codes of conduct and operating standards, under the guidance of national regulatory authorities, to improve service quality. Transparent, simple, and inexpensive out-of-court procedures resolve disputes involving consumers in a fair and prompt manner, alongside systems of reimbursement and compensation.

The Directive aims to provide a framework for the exploitation of public information to ensure that competition in the internal market is not distorted. It recognizes that digital content plays an important role in an information and knowledge society. The framework, however, is not mandatory and the decision whether or not to authorize re-use will remain with the Member States or the public sector body concerned.

The Directive exlude specific types of documents from its scope, including activities falling outside the scope of the public task, documents for which third parties hold intellectual property rights, documents which are excluded from access, documents held by public service broadcasters and their subsidiaries, documents held by educational and research establishments, and documents held by cultural establishments. The Directive also maintain the protections given by the data protection directive.

The Member States must ensure that where the re-use of documents held by public sector bodies is allowed, these documents shall be re-usable for commercial or non-commercial purposes under the conditions set by the Directive. Requestes for re-use should be answered within 20 working days, and extented by 20 working days, unless stated otherwise. in cases of refusal, the public body must also communicate the grounds for refusal and refer to the means for redress.
Documents should be accessible in existing formats or languages via electronic means. Public bodies aren't required to produce specific document types for reuse by private or public organizations..

Fees cannot exceed the cost of collection, production, reproduction, and dissemintation.

Public sector bodies may allow for re-use of documents without conditions or may impose conditions, where appropriate, through a license, dealing with relevant issues. These conditions shall not unnecessarily restrict possibilities for re-use and shall not be used to restrict competition.

Any applicable conditions for the re-use of documents shall be non-discriminatory for comparable categories of re-use.

The re-use of documents shall be open to all potential actors in the market, even if one or more market players already exploit added-value products based on these documents. However, where an exclusive right is necessary for the provision of a service in the public interest, the validity of the reason for granting such an exclusive right shall be subject to regular review, and shall, in any event, be reviewed every three years. The exclusive arrangements established after the entry into force of this Directive shall be transparent and made public.

The Directive starts by stating in Receital 1 that "The achievement of the Internal Market entails eliminating restrictions on freedom of movement and distortions of competition, while creating an environment conducive to innovation and investment. In this context, the protection of intellectual property is an essential element for the success of the Internal Market. The protection of intellectual property is important not only for promoting innovation and creativity, but also for developing employment and improving competitiveness."

The Directive objective is to regulate the measures, procedures and remedies necessary to ensure the enforcement of intellectual property rights.

Member States must provide fair, effective, and proportionate measures, procedures, and remedies to enforce intellectual property rights, ensuring they are not overly complicated, costly, or delayed, and avoiding barriers to legitimate trade or abuse.

The Directive requires the recognition of both holders of IPR and persons authorized to use those rights, as well as IP collective rights management bodies which are regularly recognized as having a right to represent holders of intellectual property rights and professional defense bodies.

The Directive’s core governance model is therefore court-centred private enforcement under a harmonised public framework, supplemented by limited industry self-regulation. Member States construct the enforcement framework, national courts exercise coercive enforcement, and rightholders and their representative organisations activate that enforcement. The Commission coordinates and evaluates, while industry associations supplement the regime through codes of conduct.
column17: The Directive operationalised self-regulation by requiring Member States to encourage trade and professional associations to develop EU-level codes of conduct supporting intellectual-property enforcement, particularly through product-identification measures. Associations were also encouraged to submit draft codes and evaluations to the Commission. These voluntary industry measures supplemented a predominantly court-centred enforcement regime backed by injunctions, corrective measures, and damages

The Regulation creates ENISA as an advisory and coordinating agency. It regulates the Agency’s governance, work programme, finances, transparency, staffing, and accountability. Although ENISA assists the Commission, Member States, and national authorities with network-security policy, it does not adopt binding standards, supervise compliance, or impose sanctions.

Regulation 460/2004 establishes ENISA as an EU advisory and coordinating agency for network and information security. Its strategic direction, annual work programme, budget, and internal rules are determined by a Management Board composed primarily of voting representatives from each Member State and the Commission, while its Executive Director manages its daily operations and implements the Board’s decisions. Industry, consumer, and academic representatives participate through non-voting Board membership, the Permanent Stakeholders’ Group, and ad hoc working groups. ENISA collects and analyses security risks, advises EU and national authorities, promotes common methodologies and best practices, monitors standardisation developments, and facilitates dialogue with industry. It cannot adopt binding rules, compel information disclosure, inspect regulated organisations, determine compliance, order corrective action, or impose sanctions. Regulatory and enforcement authority therefore remains with the Commission, Member States, and competent national authorities under other EU and national legislation.

The Commission Regulation sets out the public policy rules concerning the implementation and functions of the .eu Top Level Domain (TLD) and the public policy principles on registration.

The Commission determines the principal public-policy and registration rules, while the non-profit Registry administers the regime. The Registry accredits and contracts with registrars, specifies technical requirements, manages registrations, verifies eligibility, establishes revocation procedures, and selects validation agents, auditors, escrow agents, and ADR providers. Its discretion is substantial but bounded by detailed legal requirements of transparency, objectivity, non-discrimination, competition, procedural fairness, and Commission oversight and decisions by courts of the Member States. 

The Regulation specifies what should be included in the requests to register domain names. 

Courts of the Member States can decide that a domain name is defamtory, racist, or contary to public policy, leading to it being blocked and revokation upon notification.
column17:
The Regulation also describe the procedure to accredit of registrars by the Registry. That procedure should be reasonable, transparent and non-discriminatory, and shall ensure effective and fair conditions of competition. The registrars may submit applications only after the date of accreditation. 
Self-regulation was operationalised through the delegation of .eu domain administration to a non-profit Registry. Within a detailed public framework, the Registry accredited and contracted with registrars, established technical and procedural requirements, administered registration and revocation, and selected validation, audit, escrow, and dispute-resolution intermediaries. Registrars implemented these requirements through their contractual relationships with registrants, while independent intermediaries verified claims and resolved disputes.

The registry shall select validation agents, which are legal persons which are reputable bodies with appropriate expertise that assess the right which is claimed for a particular name.  The registry must select the validation agents in an objective, transparent and non-discriminatory manner, ensuring the widest possible geographical diversity (Article 13). The validation agents verify by documentary evidence and examine the applications for any particular domain name in the order in which the application was received at the Registry. The relevant validation agent shall examine whether the applicant that is first in line to be assessed for a domain name and that has submitted the documentary evidence before the deadline has prior rights on the name. 

The Registry must also enter into agreement with an escrow agent to ensure continuity of service, and in particular to ensure that in the event of re-delegation or other unforeseen circumstances it is possible to continue to provide services to the local Internet community with minimum disruption. Article 15 describe the terms and conditions that should be included in the agreement, with the Commission giving its consent to the agreement before it is concluded. 

An independent auditor performs an audit to confirm the fair, appropriate and sound operational and technical administration of the phased registration period at the end of the phased registration and report its findings to the Commission (Article 12).

ADR is mandatory on the holder of a domain name and the registry and is paid for by the compliantant. The ADR providers are reputable bodies with appropriate expertise in an objective, transparent and non-discriminatory manner and selected by the Registry. A dispute which is submitted to the ADR procedure shall be examined by arbitrators appointed to a panel of one or three members. A panellist shall be impartial and independent and shall have, before accepting appointment, disclosed to the provider any circumstances giving rise to justifiable doubt as to their impartiality or independence.

Member States must ensure that comptent authorities have adequate resources and that their officials observe professional standards and internal procedures or rules of conduct, in particular, regarding the processing of personal data, procedural fairness, and the proper observance of the confidentiality and professional secrecy provisions.

The Commission will publish the list of liaison offices and competent authorities. The Commission also maintains the database, which shall be made avaliable for consultation only by competent authorities. 

Competent authorities may ask for mutual assistance from another competent authority through the designated information exchange procedures through the liasion office.

Member States must also inform each other and the Commission on community activities, including training of their consumer protection enforcement officials, collection and classification of consumer complaints, development of sector-specific networks of competent officials, development of information and communication tools, development of standards, methodologies and guidelines for consumer protection enforcement officials, and the exchange of their officials. The competent authorities may exchange competent officials in order to improve cooperation.

The Member States must also inform one another and the Commission of their activities regarding consumer information and advice, support of the activities of consumer representatives, support of consumers' access to justice, and collection of statistics, the results of research or other information relating to consumer behaviour, attitudes and outcomes.

The Commission is supported by a Committee and reports on the implementation, as well as any new information about the organisation, powers, resources or responsibilities of the competent authorities, 	
any information concerning trends, means or methods of committing intra-Community infringements, any information on enforcement techniques, summary statistics relating to the activities of competent authorities, 
summaries of significant national interpretative judgments, and any other information relevant for the application of the Regulation.

The Directive lists several exclusive rights, including distribution rights, a right associated with broadcasting and communication to the public, a fixation right, and the right to authorise or prohibit rental and lending of their work, performance, phonograpm, and films, allowing them to transfer, assigning or subject them to contracts (subject to the right to equitable remuneration).

The administration of the right to obtain remuneration may be entrusted to collecting societies representing authors or performers. Member States may regulate whether and to what extent administration by collecting societies of the right to obtain an equitable remuneration may be imposed, as well as the question from whom this remuneration may be claimed or collected.

Member States may place limitation on some of the rights, in respect to private use, use of short excerpts for reporting of events, ephemeral fixation, and to use solely for the purposes of teaching or scientific research.

Member states must communicate to the Commission the main provisions of national law they adopted.

This Directive was enacted due to new audiovisual transmission technologies, requiring a regulatory update to address structural changes, the spread of information and communication technologies (ICT) and technological developments affecting business models, especially commercial broadcasting funding. It aims to ensure competitive, certain conditions for Europe’s ICT and media industries while respecting cultural and linguistic diversity. It amended the Television Without Frontier Directive.

Traditional audiovisual media services — such as television — and emerging on-demand audiovisual media services offer significant employment opportunities in the Community, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises, and stimulate economic growth and investment. 

	
"On 15 December 2003, the Commission adopted a Communication on the future of European regulatory audiovisual policy, in which it stressed that regulatory policy in that sector has to safeguard certain public interests, such as cultural diversity, the right to information, media pluralism, the protection of minors and consumer protection and to enhance public awareness and media literacy, now and in the future. 	
The Resolution of the Council and of the Representatives of the Governments of the Member States, meeting within the Council of 25 January 1999 concerning public service broadcasting (9) reaffirmed that the fulfilment of the mission of public service broadcasting requires that it continue to benefit from technological progress. The co-existence of private and public audiovisual media service providers is a feature which distinguishes the European audiovisual media market.

(10)

The Commission has adopted the initiative ‘i2010: European Information Society’ to foster growth and jobs in the information society and media industries. This is a comprehensive strategy designed to encourage the production of European content, the development of the digital economy and the uptake of ICT, against the background of the convergence of information society services and media services, networks and devices, by modernising and deploying all EU policy instruments: regulatory instruments, research and partnerships with industry. The Commission has committed itself to creating a consistent internal market framework for information society services and media services by modernising the legal framework for audiovisual services." 

This Directive does not alter Member States' obligations under Directive 98/34/EC of 22 June 1998, which establishes procedures for information on technical standards and regulations, including rules on Information Society services. Therefore, any draft national measures for on-demand audiovisual media services that are more stringent or detailed than what is needed to transpose this Directive should follow the procedural requirements of Article 8 of Directive 98/34/EC.
Furthermore, Directive 2002/21/EC of 7 March 2002, known as the Framework Directive, which establishes a common regulatory framework for electronic communications networks and services, does not affect measures taken at the Community or national level aimed at pursuing general interest objectives, especially in content regulation and audiovisual policy, as per its Article 1(3). This Directive does not require or promote Member States to introduce new licensing or administrative authorization systems for any type of audiovisual media service.

Member States must ensure all audiovisual service providers comply with their laws applicable to media services for the public in that Member State. They cannot restrict retransmission of services from other Member States. They may prevent on-demand services for public policy, health, security, or consumer protection reasons if such services threaten these objectives or pose serious risks, and such measures must be proportionate. They also need to first ask the other Member State to take take measures and notify the Commission and the other MS of its intention to take measures. The Commission needs to examine the compatability of these measures against community law in the shortest possible time, and if it finds they are not compatible, it can ask the MS to refrain from taking any proposed measures or urgently to put an end to these measures. 

MS can require providers to comply with more detailed or stricter rules in field coordindated under this Directive, provided that these rules comply with Community law. However, where an MS adopts such rules and assesses that a broadcaster in another MS provides services in its territory, it may contact the other MS in order to achieve a mutually satisfactory solution. That other MS shall request the broadcaster to comply with the rules o genaral public interest in questions and inform the first MS of the results. It the first MS is not statisfied, it many adopt appropriate measures against the broadcaster and those measure shall be objectively necessary, applied in a non-discriminatory manner and be proportionate to the objectives which they pursue. It must first notify the Commission and other other member states of these measures and its ground for substaintiating its assessment and the Commission has decided that the measures are compatible with Community Law and that assessment are correctly founded. If the Commission decided that the meausres are incompatable, the MS shall refrain from taking these measures. 

The Directive maintain the provisions of Directive 2000/31 yet have precedence over it in cases of conflict.

MS must also take appropriate measures to ensure that on-demand services that might seriously impair the physical, mental or moral development of minors are only made available in such a way that ensures that minors will not normally hear or see such on-demand audiovisual media servic They must also ensure that on-deman services promote where practicable and by appropriate means, the production of European Works. Such promotion could relate, inter alia, to the financial contribution made by such services to the production and rights acquisition of European works or to the share and/or prominence of European works in the catalogue of programmes offered by the on-demand audiovisual media service.

They must also ensure that events with major importance are not broadcast exclusively in a way that deprive a substantial proportion of the public in that Member State of the possibility of following such events by live coverage or deferred coverage on free television. MS may also draw up a list of designated events which it considers to be of major importance for society, to determine whether these events should be available by whole or partial live or deffered coverage. They will then notify the Commission of these measures it will verify compliance with Community law and communicate the measures to other MSs, followed by formal publication in the OJEU.
MS must ensure that any broadcaster may access on a fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory basis events of high interest, even when transmitted on an exlclusive basis, for the purpose of short news reports. Broadcasters may freely choose short extracts from the transmitting broadcaster while identifying the source. 

 
MS shall take appropriate measure to provide each other and the Commission with the information necessary for the application of the directive. And the Commission will report on its implementation every three years and make proposals to adapt it based on developments in the field of audiovisual media services, in particular in the light of recent technological developments.

The Directive defined audiovisual media service more clearly as a service under the editorial responsibility of a media service provider and the principal purpose of which is the provision of programmes in order to inform, entertain or educate, to the general public by electronic communications networks. It can be either televisison broadcaster, and on-demnad audiovisual media service, or audiovisual commercial communication.

The Directive also more clearly describe editorial responsibility as the exercise of effective control both over the selection of the programmes and over their organisation either in a chronological schedule, in the case of television broadcasts, or in a catalogue, in the case of on-demand audiovisual media services. Editorial responsibility does not necessarily imply any legal liability under national law for the content or the services provided;
Similarly, the directive also described "media service provider" as the natural or legal person who has editorial responsibility for the choice of the audiovisual content and “television broadcasting” or “television broadcast” (i.e. a linear audiovisual media service) means an audiovisual media service provided by a media service provider for simultaneous viewing of programmes on the basis of a programme schedule;

The Directive also clarified the meaning of European Works

MS are in charge to make sure media service providers effectively comply with this Directive, and shall encourage co- and/or self-regulatory regimes at national level in the fields coordinated by this Directive to the extent permitted by their legal systems. These regimes shall be such that they are broadly accepted by the main stakeholders in the Member States concerned and provide for effective enforcement.

There are clearer prescriptive rules, which leaves room for process-based regulation:
MS must ensure providers give mandatory info about themselves and authorities, avoid hate speech, be accessible for disabled people, comply with rights holders' periods, and make commercial communications recognizable without subliminal techniques. They should respect human dignity, avoid discrimination, health risks, or environmental harm. Prohibitions include ads for tobacco, alcohol to minors, excessive drinking, and prescription medicines.

MS and the Commission can encourage media service providers to develop codes of conduct on inappropriate audiovisual commercials in children's programs about foods and drinks with nutrients like fat, trans fats, salt, and sugars, which should be consumed in moderation.

Sponsored services must not impact media provider's independence or encourage purchases, especially by promotional references, and must clearly disclose sponsorship. Sponsorship by tobacco manufacturers or for prescription medicines is prohibited. News and current affairs programs cannot be spoProduct placement is prohibited unless a Member State decides otherwise, under conditions: (a) content and scheduling must not influence media provider's responsibility or independence; (b) they must not directly encourage purchase or rental with promotional references; (c) they must not give undue prominence to the product; (d) viewers must be clearly informed of product placement, with programmes appropriately identified at start, end, and after breaks to prevent confusion.

Programmes shall not include product placement of tobacco, cigarettes, or from companies mainly selling tobacco, nor specific medicinal products only available by prescription in the Member State where the media service provider operates fall.

Broadcasters must also seperate and isolate television ads and teleshopping from editorial content, except for sports events.Where tv ads is inserted during programs, the integrity of the programms and the rights of right holder should not be prejudiced.

The proportion of tv ads spots shall not exceed 20% of an hour, and clearly identifiable, unless the channel is exclusively devoted to ads.

The Directive sets the rules for regulating payment service providers. The Directive applies where a telecommunications or IT operator acts only as an intermediary between the user and the supplier. It does not apply where the operator plays a substantive role in producing, distributing, providing access to, or enabling the use of digital goods or services. The distinction is therefore functional, not simply technological:
If the operator performs a payment function, the activity is regulated as a payment service.
If the payment is embedded in the operator’s provision or distribution of digital content, it falls outside this Directive.

Organisation should hold their own initial capital and own funds, with the Directive setting three methods for MS and competent authorities to choose how to determine how many funds payment institutions must hold:i a percentage of the previous year’s fixed overheads (Method A), a progressively weighted share of annual payment volume (Method B), or a progressively weighted income-based indicator (Method C). The competent authority determines which method applies and may adjust the resulting requirement in accordance with to the institution’s risk management and internal controls.

Article 10 requires competent authorities to grant authorisation where the institution meets the Directive’s requirements and has sound governance, internal controls, and risk-management arrangements. They must withdraw it only where the institutions does not make use of the authorisation within 12 months, has obtained the authorisation through false statements or any irregular means, no longer fulfils the conditions for granting the authorisation,  would constitute a threat to the stability of the payment system, or falls within one of the other cases where national law provides for withdrawal of an authorisation.

MS manges their national registry of authorised payment institutions (not the Commission).

Competent authorities are designated by the MS, and they must remain independent, avoid conflict of interests, and possess the necessary powers. MS must ensure that controls exercised the authories are proportionate, adequate, and responsive to the risk to which payment institutions are exposed. They may ask for information, carry out inspections, issue recommendations and guidelines, binding administrative provisions, and suspend or withdraw authorisation. They may also impose penalties or measures against institutions or who effectively controls them.  Meanwhile, employees of the competent authories must maintain professional secrecy, and authorities may cooperate with one antoher or the European Central Bank or national cetnral banks.

MS must inform the Commission in cases it provides waivers of the application of all or part of the procedure and conditions.

MS must also ensure that the rules on access of authorized or registered payment service providers that are legal persons to payment systems shall be objective, non-discriminatory and proportionate and that those rules do not inhibit access more than is necessary to safeguard against specific risks such as settlement risk, operational risk and business risk and to protect the financial and operational stability of the payment system. 

Title IV, then requires the MS to establish the mandatory rules governing authorization, security, execution, refunds, and liability, while Member States transpose these rules and make several specified choices. Payment service providers implement these rules through contracts and transaction-management decisions. They have limited contractual discretion, such as agreeing on consent procedures, spending limits, notification methods, certain charges, and specific derogations for non-consumers or low-value instruments. Providers also implement some process-based requirements:  they must authenticate and record transactions (Article 59), may block instruments on specified security or risk grounds (Article 55), must prevent further use following notification of loss, theft, misappropriation, or unauthorized use (Articles 56–57), and must trace non-executed or defectively executed transactions upon request (Article 75).

MS must ensure that users and other interested parties may submit complaints to the competent authorities. They must notify the Commission of the competent authority they appoint. They must also ensure that adequate and effective out-of-court complaint and redress procedures for the settlement of disputes between payment service users and their payment service providers are put in place.

The Commission is also tasked with revewing the Directive

The directive sets in Article 5 the information applicants must submit to national competent authroties, which sets the process-based boudaries in which the opeate. The must provide program of operation, business plans, prove of capital, measures to safeguard users' funds. They also have to describe their internal arrangements and control mechanisms for roportionate, appropriate, sound and adequate administrative, risk management and accounting procedures, as well as mechanisms to comply with money laudnering and terrorist financing obligations. Under this, providers may also describe their structural organization and the identy of directors and persons responsible for the management of the payment institution and, where relevant, persons responsible for the management of the payment services activities of the payment institution, as well as evidence that they are of good repute and possess appropriate knowledge and experience to perform payment services.
 They should also provide a description of its audit arrangements and the organisational arrangements it has set up with a view to taking all reasonable steps to protect the interests of its users and to ensure continuity and reliability in the performance of payment services.

Article 9 further requires payment institutions to safeguard users’ funds either by segregating and protecting them from creditors or through insurance or a comparable guarantee. In this latter option, an insurance company or a credit institution, which does not belong to the same group as the payment institution itself, for an amount equivalent to that which would have been segregated in the absence of the insurance policy or other comparable guarantee.

Auditors must audit the annual accounts and consolidated accounts of payment institutions.

When payment institutions provide payment services through an agent, they must communicate relevant information to the Competent authority, yet the competent authorities may refuse to regiter agents. 

MS must ensure that payment institutions remain fully liable for any acts of their employees, or any agent, branch or entity to which activities are outsourced (which is opposed to the liability regime under the e-commerce Directive). The payment institutions must all keep all appropriate records.

The Directive also prescribe transperancy rules regarding conditions and information requirement for payment services, and inparticular, single payment transactions, framework contracts.  Payment service providers may not charge payments for providing information, yet may charge for additional or more frequent information when the user agrees.  

Providers also implement some process-based requirements:  they must authenticate and record transactions (Article 59), may block instruments on specified security or risk grounds (Article 55), must prevent further use following notification of loss, theft, misappropriation, or unauthorized use (Articles 56–57), and must trace non-executed or defectively executed transactions upon request (Article 75). Processing of personal data must follow the rules set by the data protection directive.

The directive addresses police and judicial cooperation, and specifically, the exchange of personal data within this framework. It ensures a high level of protection of the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, and in particular their right to privacy, with respect to the processing of personal data. MS must protect fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, and in particular their right to privacy when, for the purpose of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, personal data is transmitted between MS. The Directive also applies to processing of personal data wholly or partly by automatic means.

Similar to the Data Protection Directive, personal data may only be collected by the competent authorities only for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes in the framework of their tasks, and further processing should be compatible withthe purposes for which it was collected, the other purpose is in accordance with applicable law, and it necessary and proportionate to the other purpoese.

Principles of rectification, erasure, and blocking apply with the applicable changes, and time limits shall be establish for erasing data. Processing of special categories of data shall be permitted only when this is strictly necessary and when the national law provides adequate safeguards,

solely automated processing of data to evalue certain personal aspects relating to the data subject shall be permitted only if authorised by a law which also lays down measures to safeguard the data subject’s legitimate interests

 The competent authorities shall take all reasonable steps to provide that personal data which are inaccurate, incomplete or no longer up to date are not transmitted or made available; If it emerges that incorrect data have been transmitted or data have been unlawfully transmitted, the recipient must be notified without delay.

All transmissions of personal data are to be logged or documented/ Personal data from another Member State's authority can only be further processed for specific purposes beyond those initially transmitted, including criminal proceedings, judicial or administrative actions related to criminal activities, preventing serious threats to public security, or with prior consent from the transmitting Member State or data subjects as per national law. Authorities may also process data for historical, statistical, or scientific purposes if safeguards are in place anonymous.

The Framework also set rules about transferring data to competent authorities in third States or to international bodies, as well as to private parties in MS. 

The framework decision also provides personal rights, including the rights to information, access, rectification, erasure or blocking, right to compensation, and right for judicial rememdies.

MS must ensure authorities implement measures to protect personal data from accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised access, especially during transmission or automated access, considering processing risks and data nature. The MS must also implement measure regarding equiptment access control , data media control, storage control, user control, data access control, communication contol, input control, transport control, recovery, and integrity. 

Competent national supervisory authorities shall be consulted prior to the processing of personal data. MS must appoint at least one supervisory authorities and award them with investigative powers, powers of intervention, and power to engance in legal proceeding. They will also hear claims lodge by any person.

This regulation directly regulates regulatory intermediaries, and particularly the accreditation of conformity assessment bodies and the general principles for the CE marking. It provides provides a framework for the market surveillance of products to ensure that those products fulfil requirements providing a high level of protection of public interests. It also refers to harmonised standard linking them to the European standardisation bodies listed in Directive 98/34/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 June 1998 laying down a procedure for the provision of information in the field of technical standards and regulations and of rules on Information Society services.

Accreditation an attestation by a national accreditation body that a conformity assessment body meets the requirements set by harmonised standards and, where applicable, any additional requirements including those set out in relevant sectoral schemes, to carry out a specific conformity assessment activity.

‘conformity assessment’ now more broadly mean the process demonstrating whether specified requirements relating to a product, process, service, system, person or body have been fulfilled, with conformity assessment body emaning a body that performs conformity assessment activities including calibration, testing, certification and inspection (which means it covers also testing laboratories).

The Regulation also recognize the process of peer evaluation, meaning the assessment of a national accreditation body by other national accreditation bodies.

Market surveillance authorities are now also defined as an authority of a Member State responsible for carrying out activities carried out and measures to ensure that products comply with the requirements set out in the relevant Community harmonisation legislation and do not endanger health, safety or any other aspect of public interest protection.

The regulation requires MS to appoint a single national accreditation bodies to conduct compulsory or voluntary accredtiatinos in their territories or decide to rely on another MS. The Commssion draw up the list of NAB. Where accreditation is not operated directly by the public authorities themselves, a Member State shall entrust its national accreditation body with the operation of accreditation. NABs must be clearly distinguish from other national authorites and operate on a not-for-proft basis. It may not provide any conformity assessment services that CABs provide or proivde consultancy services.

The National Accreditation Body (NAB) evaluates the competence of Conformity Assessment Bodies (CABs) to perform conformity assessments and issue accreditation certificates. Member States (MS) could opt not to use accreditation and can provide the necessary documentation to the European Commission for verifying CAB competence.


NABs may not comptete with CABs or other NABs.

NABs must remain independent from the CABs they assess to ensure objectivity. Different, competent individuals should make decisions separate from those who conducted the assessment. They must maintain confidentiality, efficient management, and internal controls, employing qualified personnel. Staff duties and responsibilities should be documented, and performance must be monitored. NABs should ensure that conformity assessments are suitable for the size, sector, complexity, and nature of the undertaking, and publish audited annual accounts according to accepted accounting principles.

Member States (MS) are responsible for ensuring that National Accreditation Bodies (NABs) comply with regulations and must take corrective actions if they do not. They need to monitor activities and consider peer evaluations managed by a recognized body under Article 14. While stakeholders supervise these evaluations, they do not participate. Evaluations must adhere to transparent criteria regarding structural, human resource, and process requirements, confidentiality, and complaints, to confirm NAB compliance with relevant harmonized standards. NABs that meet these standards and pass peer evaluations are considered to fulfill their obligations.


The Commission oversees the peer evaluation system and must finalize an agreement detailing tasks, funding, and supervision. It may request contributions for developing and implementing accreditation, as well as establishing evaluation criteria and sectoral accreditation schemes, including accepting existing schemes. The European cooperation for accreditation is directly mentioned in the regulation, and the Regulation describes which of its activities the Community may finance. Annex I further describes the requirements of this body.

COMMUNITY MARKET SURVEILLANCE FRAMEWORK :
MS are in charge to organise and carry out market surveillance activities. The Regulation set the applicable provisions, in so far as there are no specific provisions with the same objective in the specific legislation. The must inform the Commission of their market surveillance authorities and their area of competence. They must ensure these authorities can communicate and coordinate; MS must esnure procedures for following up compliants aor reports regarding risks, monitor accidents, verify that corrective action has been taken, and 	
follow up scientific and technical knowledge concerning safety issues. They must entrust their  market surveillance authorities with the powers, resources and knowledge necessary for the proper performance of their tasks. Member States shall also establish, implement and periodically update their market surveillance programmes

Meanwhile the Regulation requires market surveillance authorities to perform appropriate checks on the characteristics of products on an adequate scale, by means of documentary checks and, where appropriate, physical and laboratory checks on the basis of adequate samples. They can require information and documentation as well as enter the premises and take samples. They should warn users of hazards. They must act independently, impartially and without bias. MSA may also order authorities in charge of border control to include statements that the product is dangerous and not authorised for circulation.

MS, not just MSA, must ensure that prodict with serious risks are recalled and that the Commission is informed. Decisions to prohibit or restrict product must be proportionate and state the exact grounds on which it is based. The economic operator must be given appropriate time to respond.

The Commission is notified through the Community Rapid Information System under Directive 2001/95/EC. The Commission needs also to develop and manage a general archiving and exchange of information system.
MS and their MSAs need to cooperate among themselves as well as with the Commission and the Community agencies. The Commission may also develop initatives to share resources and expertise, including taining, and programs to share  experience, information and best practice.
