The Decision sets out common principles and references for drawing up Community harmonisation legislation. Community harmonisation legislation must be restricted to setting out essential requirements determining the level of protection and must express those requirements in terms of the results to be achieved. Harmonized standards adopted in accordance with Directive 98/34/EC may translate and express those requirements in technical terms and shall, alone or in conjunction with other harmonized standards, provide a presumption of conformity with those requirements. 

Article 4: selection of conformity assessment procedures:
Where Community harmonisation legislation requires conformity assessment, Article 4 requires the applicable procedures to be selected from the modules set out in Annex II based on: (a) the appropriateness of the module for the product; (b) the risks presented by the product and whether the conformity assessment corresponds to the type and degree of risk; (c) where third-party involvement is mandatory, the need to provide manufacturers with a choice between quality assurance and product certification; and (d) the need to avoid imposing burdensome modules relative disproportionate to the risks covered by the legislation.

Article 5: EC declaration of conformity
Where Community harmonisation legislation requires a manufacturer’s statement of conformity, the legislation must specify that a single EC declaration of conformity covers all relevant Community acts. This declaration should include all information necessary to identify the applicable Community harmonisation legislation, together with the relevant publication references.

Article 6: Actors performing conformity assessment
The Decision specifies that conformity assessments may be conducted by public authorities, manufacturers, or notified bodies. When Community harmonisation legislation mandates that conformity assessments be performed by public authorities, it must also stipulate that the CABsthese authorities rely on for technical assessments meet the same criteria as notified bodies.

Responsibilities of the Member States and the Commission concerning harmonised standards
Article R9: Formal objections to harmonized standards
Annex I also sets rules regarding standardization. It permits MS and the Commission to bring matters before the designated committee where they consider that harmonized standards do not entirely satisfy the requirements. After the Committee provides its opinion, the Commission may decide to publish, maintain, restrict, or withdraw references to the relevant harmonized standards. It must inform the relevant European standardisation body and request it to revise the standard.

Responsibilities of Member States and notifying authorities
Articles R13–R15: Notifying authorities
Annex I defines rules for notifying authorities and bodies. It requires member states to appoint notifying authorities responsible for establishing and carrying out procedures for assessing, notifying conformity assessment bodies, and monitoring notified bodies. Member States may decide that national accreditation bodies perform assessment and monitoring.

Notifying authorities must be organized so that conflicts of interest with conformity-assessment bodies are avoided. They must operate objectively and impartially, ensure that notification decisions are taken by persons other than those conducting the assessment, refrain from providing conformity-assessment or consultancy services, and preserve confidentiality. Member States must inform the Commission of their procedures for the assessment and notification of conformity-assessment bodies and the monitoring of notified bodies. MS must inform the Commission of their procedures for assessment and notification of CABs. 

Articles R22–R26: Notification process
When applying for notification, a conformity-assessment body must submit a description of its conformity-assessment activities, relevant modules, and products, along with an accreditation certificate from a national accreditation body, where one exists, attesting that it complies with Article R17. Where no accreditation certificate is available, the body must provide the documentary evidence necessary to verify and regularly monitor its compliance.

The notifying authority must then notify the Commission and other Member States of the assessment activities, modules, products, and relevant attestation of competence. The body may operate as a notified body only if the Commission and the other Member States raise no objections within two weeks where accreditation is used or within two months where it is not.

Where a notifying authority ascertains ascertains that a notified body no longer meets the requirements, it must restrict, suspend, or withdraw the notificiation notification, as appropriate, and inform the Commission and the other Member States. The Commission may also investigate whether a notified body is competent and continues to meet its requirements and responsibilities. It may request the notifying authority to take necessary measures, including withdrawal of the notification. 

Responsbilities of CABS and notified bodies
 CABs. 

Articles R17–R18: Requirements applicable to notified bodies
For notification purposes, conformity-assessment bodies must be independent of the organization or product they assess; top management and personnel involved in conformity assessments must not design, manufacture, supply, install, purchase, own, use, or maintain the products assessed. They must avoid activities that threaten their independence f judgement or the integrity of their assessment activities. 
CABs must also conduct assessments professionally and with technical competence, free from pressures or inducements that could affect judgment. They must have qualified personnel, transparent procedures, and sufficient resources, taking account of the organization's size, sector, and complexity. Personnel must have appropriate technical training, satisfactory knowledge of the applicable essential requirements and standards, and be capable of drawing out certificates, records, and reports showing assessments were carried out. 
CABs and their personnel must observe professional confidentiality and participate in relevant standardization activities and the notified body coordination group established under the relevant Community legislation. If CABs meet the criteria in a harmonized standard referenced in the OJEU, they are presumed to comply with the requirements covered by that standard.

Articles R27–R28: Operational and information obligations
Notified bodies must carry out the fity assessments proportionately, avoid unnecessary burdens, and consider the size and structure of the undertaking, its sector, the complexity of the relevant product technology, and the nature of the production process. They shall must nevertheless respect the required degree of rigour and level of protection. They may require corrective actions and can must, where appropriate, refuse, restrict, suspend, or withdraw certificates.

They must inform the notifying authorities of certificates refused, restricted, suspended, or withdrawn, circumstances affecting the scope or conditions of notification, requests received from market-surveillance authorities, and, on request, conformity-assessment activities performed. They must also provide other notified bodies conducting similar activities for the same products with relevant information concerning negative and, on request, positive conformity-assessment results.

Responsibilities of the Commission and Member States for coordination
Article R29: Exchange of experience
The Commission must organise the exchange of experience among Member States’ national authorities responsible for notification policy.

Article R30: Coordination of notified bodies
The Commission must ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between notified bodies through one or more sectoral or cross-sectoral groups. Member States must ensure that their notified bodies participate in these groups, either directly or through designated representatives.

Responsibilities concerning market surveillance and products presenting risks
Articles R31 and R33: Products presenting risks
If non-compliance is attributed to shortcommings in a harmonised standard, the Commissiom must inform the relevant European standardisation body and bring the matter before the committee referred to in Article R9. Article R33 establishes a separate procedure where a product complies with the applicable legislation but nevertheless presents a risk to health or safety or to another aspect of public-interest protection.

Article R34: Formal non-compliance
Additionally, where a Member State makes one of the following findings, it shall require the relevant economic operator to put an end to the non-compliance concerned:
(a) the conformity marking has been affixed in violation of Article [R11] or [R12];
(b) the conformity marking has not been affixed;
(c) the EC declaration of conformity has not been drawn up;
(d) the EC declaration of conformity has not been drawn up correctly;
(e) technical documentation is either not available or not complete.

Where the non-compliance referred to in paragraph 1 persists, the Member State concerned shall take all appropriate measures to restrict or prohibit the product being made available on the market or ensure that it is recalled or withdrawn from the market.
Annex II:
Annex II establishes a graduated system for allocating conformity-assessment responsibilities among manufacturers, accredited in-house bodies, and notified bodies. The modules differ according to the stage of assessment, the functions assigned to each actor, and the intensity of independent verification. They cover both product design and production, and range from manufacturer self-assessment to comprehensive third-party examination, certification, and surveillance. 

Annex II creates a continuum between manufacturer self-assessment and extensive third-party assurance. 
Module A relies entirely on internal production control. The remaining modules allocate progressively more extensive assurance functions to notified bodies.

Manufacturers remain responsible for product conformity, technical documentation, production controls, the declaration of conformity, and the conformity marking. Third-party assurance supplements and verifies organisational compliance but does not transfer the manufacturer’s legal responsibility to the notified body.

Notified bodies perform several distinct regulatory functions. Depending on the applicable module, they examine product designs or types, conduct or supervise testing, approve quality systems, undertake periodic audits and unannounced visits, verify individual products or samples, and issue certificates or quality-system approvals. They may also refuse, restrict, suspend, or withdraw certificates and approvals where conformity has not been demonstrated or maintained. Their role consequently extends beyond technical testing to continuing assurance and control over access to the market.
Accredited in-house bodies occupy an intermediate position between manufacturer self-assessment and independent third-party assessment. They remain part of the undertaking but must constitute a separate and identifiable organisational unit, demonstrate impartiality through accreditation, and provide their services exclusively to the undertaking of which they form part. Their involvement allows specified testing and verification functions to remain internal while subjecting those functions to external accreditation requirements.

The manufacturer also does not determine the institutional arrangement autonomously. Sectoral harmonisation legislation selects the permissible conformity-assessment modules according to the type of product, the nature and degree of risk, and the appropriate intensity of third-party involvement. Where several modules are permitted, the manufacturer may choose among them and select a competent notified body, but only within the options established by the legislation.

The applicable institutional arrangement is determined by sectoral legislation, which selects the permissible procedures according to product risk and the required degree of third-party involvement.
column17:
Although adopted as a Decision rather than a directive or regulation, Decision 2008/768 did not directly impose obligations on manufacturers, importers, and distributors. Instead, it established reference provisions for inclusion in Community harmonisation legislation. These provisions combined outcome-based requirements concerning product conformity with process-based compliance obligations. 

Under these reference provisions, manufacturers would be required to ensure that their products comply with the requirements set by the applicable sectoral legislation, draw up and keep technical documentation and the EC declaration of conformity, and carry out the applicable conformity assessment procedures. They would also have to ensure that products continued to conform, taking into account the effects of changes to product design or characteristics and to applicable harmonised standards or technical specifications.

Where appropriate in light of the risks presented by a product, manufacturers would have to conduct sample testing of marketed products, investigate complaints, and, where necessary, maintain registers of complaints, non-conforming products, and product recalls.

They would also have to ensure that the product is accompanied by instructions and safety information in a language that could be easily understood by consumers and other end-users, and immediately take corrective measures to bring non-conforming products into conformity, withdraw, or recall them. Where a product presented a risk, manufacturers would also have to inform the competent national authorities and provide details of the non-conformity and the corrective measures taken. They would further have to cooperate with competent authorities and, following a reasoned request, provide all the information and documentation necessary to demonstrate the product’s conformity.

The Decision also set general rules governing the CE marking, including responsibility for affixing it and the involvement of notified bodies where required by the applicable conformity-assessment procedure. Separate responsibilities were specified for authorised representatives, importers, and distributors.

Overall, when a manufacturer would draw an EC declaration of conformity, it would assume responsibility for the product's compliance. When the product conformed with a harmonized standard or parts of it, whose reference had been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, it would benefit from a presumption of conformity with the requirements covered by the standard or relevant parts thereof.

This captures a significant form of legally structured organizational self-regulation. Manufacturers are responsible for organising compliance, producing evidence, monitoring products, and initiating corrective action. However, their discretion operates within publicly defined requirements, while the applicable sectoral legislation determines whether self-assessment is sufficient or third-party conformity assessment is required.

column16: The Commission communication of 26 August 2010 entitled ‘A Digital Agenda for Europe’ identified the fragmentation of the digital market, the lack of interoperability and the rise in cybercrime as major obstacles to the virtuous cycle of the digital economy.

From the audiovisual directive: The Commission has adopted the initiative ‘i2010: European Information Society’ to foster growth and jobs in the information society and media industries. This is a comprehensive strategy designed to encourage the production of European content, the development of the digital economy and the uptake of ICT, against the background of the convergence of information society services and media services, networks and devices, by modernising and deploying all EU policy instruments: regulatory instruments, research and partnerships with industry. The Commission has committed itself to creating a consistent internal market framework for information society services and media services by modernising the legal framework for audiovisual services. The goal of the i2010 initiative will in principle be achieved by allowing industries to grow with only the necessary regulation, as well as allowing small start-up businesses, which are the wealth and job creators of the future, to flourish, innovate and create employment in a free market.

The directive regulates audiovisual television broadcasting, including analogue and digital television, live streaming, webcasting and near-video-on-demand, whereas video-on-demand, for example, is an on-demand audiovisual media service. The Directive does not require MS to appoint regulatory authorities; it only builds on the competent authorities the member states might already have.

Directive 2000/31/EC applies, with the current directive prevailing. It repeals Directive 89/552/EEC

The directive defines editorial responsibility as exercising effective control over programme selection and organization, whether in a schedule for TV or a catalogue for on-demand services. It does not necessarily imply legal liability for content or services.

‘media service provider’ means the person with editorial responsibility for choosing and organizing the audiovisual content of the media service.

The Directive requires Member States to ensure media service providers comply with the rules regarding their audiovisual media services; they should not restrict retransmission of audiovisual services. They may restrict services that in cases of manifestly, seriously and gravely infringes for 12 months, following a notice to the Commission and the measures they intend to take, and the Member States involved and the Commission could not settle the matter between them. 
The Commission may decide within 2 months the measures are compativel with Union Law, and may require the member states to put an end to the measures they have taken.

When it comes to on-demand audiovisual media services, MS can take measures for reasons of public policy (specifically, the prevention, investigation, detection, and prosecution of criminal offenses, e.g., protecting minors and preventing violations of human dignity), public health, public security, and consumer protection, when the measures are proportionate. Before that, the MS must inform the relevant MS, ask it to take measures, and notify the Commission.
In any case, the Commission may examine the compatibility of the notified measures, and if it concludes they do not align with Union law, it may ask the MS to refrain from taking the proposed measures. 

MS can also require providers to comply with more detailed or stricter rules, and they may contact other MS with the view to achieving mutually satisfactory solutions. They may also adopt measures against providers, but these measures hould be objectively necessary, applied in a non-discriminatory manner and proportionate to the objectives which they pursue. The MS must also inform the Commission and relevant MSs, and the Commission decided the measures comply with Union law and are correctly founded. If it decided there aren't, the MS will refrain from taking the proposed measures.

Article 14:
Member States may require major public-interest events to remain accessible on free television rather than being broadcast exclusively. They must transparently identify these events and specify whether coverage should be live, delayed, full, or partial; the list must be clear and transparent, and it shall also determine whether these events should be available by whole or partial live coverage or, where necessary or appropriate for objective reasons in the public interest, whole or partial deferred coverage.
MS must inform the Commission immediately of any measures taken, and the Commission shall verify compliance and publish the measures in OJEU.
Broadcasters must have fair access to short extracts of exclusively held public-interest events for use in general news. Member States may regulate access, length, timing, and compensation, but any fee must be limited to the direct cost of providing access.

Article 28: Broadcasters must provide a right of reply or equivalent remedy to any person whose reputation or legitimate interests have been harmed by incorrect factual assertions. The reply must be broadcast within a reasonable time and in a manner appropriate to the original programme, without unreasonable conditions. A request may be rejected if unjustified, unlawful, potentially creating civil liability, or contrary to public decency, and disputes must be subject to judicial review
column17:
The directive prescribes rules, with some performace-based criteria, that service providers must implement under their editorial responsibility and discretion.

MS can encourage self- and co-regulatory measures at the national level, with such regimes broadly accepted by the main stakeholders and effectively enforced.

Providers must make information regarding their name and address, and the identity of the competent authority, easily, directly and permanently accessible.

They musre ensure that their services do not contain any incitement to hatred based on race, sex, religion or nationality; they are encouraged to make their services accessible to people with a visual or hearing disability. They should not transmit cinematographic works outside periods agreed with the rights holders.

They must make audiovisual commercial communications recognizable, should not include subliminal techniques, and they should not 1) prejudice respect for human dignity, 2) include or promote any discrimination, 3) encourage behavior prejudicial to health or safety, and 4) encourage behaviour grossly prejudicial to the protection of the environment. Commercials for tobacco products, alcoholic beverages aimed at minors, and prescription medicine should be prohibited. Lastly, ads shall not cause physical or moral detriment to minors.

MS and the Commission may encourage media service providers to develop codes of conduct regarding inappropriate audiovisual commercial communications.

Sponsorship of services and programs must  not influence the responsibility and editorial independence, shal not directly encourage the purchase or rental of goods or services, with viewers clearly informed of the sponsorship agreement. Tabacco manufacturers and medicinal producers of prescription medicine are prohbited from sponsor or promoting their products. News and current affairs programmes shall not be sponsored.

Product placement is also prohibited, and is permitted (unless the MS prohibit them) in cinematographic works, films, series, sports, and light entertainment programs for audiovisual media, or where goods or services like props and prizes are provided free of charge for inclusion in a program.
Programs with product placement must meet these: not be influenced by it, not directly encourage purchase, not give undue prominence, and viewers must be informed of the placement.
In any case, programmes are not to contain product placement of tobacco products or prescription medicine.

Articles 12-13:
Providers of on-demand services must ensure that they do not seriously impair the physical, mental or moral development of minors and promote the production and access to European works; they may promote European works through financial contribution to the production and rights acquisition or to the share and/or prominence of European works in the catalogue of programs. MS must report on the promotion of EU works to the Commission with the Commission reporting to the Parliament and Council.

Article 16-17:
MS must ensure that broadcasters reserve for European works a majority proportion of their transmission time, excluding the time allotted to news, sports events, games, advertising, teletext services and teleshopping. This should be achieved progressively, with the MS reporting to the Commission every two years.
Broadcaster must also reserve at least 10 % of their transmission time or at least 10 % of their programming budget for European works created by producers who are independent of broadcasters; this is also to be acieved progressively, but within 5 years.

Articles 19–26: Broadcasters must ensure that advertising and teleshopping are readily recognisable and clearly distinguishable from editorial content through optical, acoustic and/or spatial means. Programme integrity and rights holders’ rights must be protected when inserting advertising, and specific limits apply to programme interruptions. Advertising and teleshopping may not exceed 20% of each clock hour. Teleshopping for medicinal products and medical treatments is prohibited, while alcohol advertising is subject to content restrictions. Teleshopping windows must be clearly identified and last at least 15 uninterrupted minutes.

Article 27: Broadcasters must not transmit programmes that may seriously impair minors, particularly pornography or gratuitous violence. Other potentially harmful content may be broadcast only when scheduling or technical safeguards normally prevent minors from accessing it. If broadcast unencoded, such content must carry an acoustic warning or a continuous visual symbol.

The Directive seeks to support the proper functioning of the internal market, including concerning digital content, meaning data which are produced and supplied in digital form, such as computer programs, applications, games, music, videos, or texts. This applies regardless of access method, whether by downloading, streaming, from a physical medium, or other means.

The Directive apply to any contract concluded between a trader and a consumer, but it does not have supremicy over other pieces of legislation. It does not apply for social services, healthcare, gambling, financial services, creation or acquistion or transfer or immovable properties, construction of new buildings,  and other legislation listed in the text. 

Member States regulate and enforce the requirements, while traders are the regulated actors. Traders must provide consumers with clear pre-contractual information on their identity, goods or services, total price, payment, delivery, guarantees, contract duration, complaints and withdrawal rights. For distance and off-premises contracts, stricter information and formal requirements apply, and consumers generally have a 14-day right of withdrawal.
Digital aspects: For digital content, traders must disclose its functionality, technical protection measures and interoperability with hardware and software. Online ordering interfaces must clearly indicate when an order creates an obligation to pay; otherwise, the consumer is not bound. Consumers bear no cost for digital content supplied during the withdrawal period unless they expressly consented to immediate performance, acknowledged losing the withdrawal right and received confirmation. The withdrawal right does not apply once supply has begun under those conditions.

Traders must also generally deliver goods within 30 days, reimburse consumers following termination for non-delivery, charge no more than their actual payment-processing costs, provide contract-related telephone lines at no more than the basic rate, and obtain express consent for additional payments rather than relying on pre-selected options. The trader generally bears the risk of loss or damage until the consumer receives the goods.

Digital aspects: The rules on payment fees, telephone charges and additional payments apply to contracts for digital content, including content supplied without a tangible medium. The delivery and passing-of-risk rules do not apply to digital content supplied without a tangible medium.

Member States must ensure that adequate and effective means exsit to ensure compliance, with one or more of the following bodies may take action under national law before the courts or before the competent administrative bodies: public bodies or their representatives, consumer protection organisations, professional organisations.

MS must also lay down rules regarding penalties and ensure they are implemented. Consumers may not waive the rights conferred to them by this directive. MS must adopt and publish the implementing laws and regulation and communicate them to the Commission. 

The Distance Contracts and the Payment Services Directives are repealed

This Regulation repeals Decison 87/95, Decision on the promotion of standardization in Europe and the preparation and implementation of standards in the field of information technology and telecommunications. It also ammends Directive 98/34/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 June 1998 laying down a procedure for the provision of information in the field of technical standards and regulations and of rules on Information Society services. This regulation is no longer just about "information society services" or about "standardisation in the field of information technology and telecommunications"

The regulation addresses the cooperation between European standardisation organisations (ESOs), national standardisation bodies (NSB), MS, and the Commission, and the establishment of European standards and deliverables in support of Union legislation. The three ESOs are CEN, CENELEC, and ETSI. MS must inform the Commission on its NSBs.

The Regulation requires ESOs and NSBs to establish annual work programs, detailing which deliverables they intends to prepare or amend. Work programs must be available. They must notify other ESOs and NSBs and the Commission. They must send any draft deliverable or standard to other ESOs, NSBs, and the Commission upom request.

ESOs should promote stakeholder representation and participation, including SMEs, consumer, environmental, and social groups, especially those financed by regulation. They must also ensure technical representation of undertakings, research centres, universities, and legal entities in emerging areas with policy or technical innovation impacts.

NSBs must encourage and facilitate the access of SMEs to standards and standards development processes, they must also exchange best practices aiming to enhance the participation of SMEs in standardisation activities.

MS must encourage participation of public authorities, including market surveillance authorities, in national standardisation activities.

The Commssion must adopt its own work program identifying strategic priorities for European standardisation. Its research facilities shall contribute to the preparation of the annual Union work program.
Article 10: It may request ESOs to draft a market-driven European standard that considers public interest, policy objectives in the Commission’s request, and consensus. It should consult with the ESOs and the organisations receicing finances. The Commission may provide funding for drafting a European standard or a European standardisation deliverable. The Commission must assess the compliance of the documents drafted by the European standardisation organisations with its initial request. And if it justify the requirement, it will publish a reference to it in the OJEU.

The MS and the Parliament can inform the Commission that standards do not entirely satisfy the requirements, and the Commission may, after consultation, decide to publish the reference with restrctions, not publish it, or withdraw the references. It may request the ESO to revise the standard. 

The Commission oalso manages the notification system for all stakeholders.

The Regulation also define the rules regarding financing of ESOs and European stakeholder organisations. The European Commission administers and supervises Union financing for standardisation. It selects funding arrangements and amounts, sets grant conditions, monitors implementation, conducts financial controls, recovers improperly paid funds and imposes penalties for irregularities. The European Court of Auditors may audit funded activities, while the European Parliament and Council exercise budgetary oversight. Union funding may also support European and national standardisation bodies and stakeholder organisations in developing, reviewing, translating and promoting standards, conducting research and conformity assessments, and participating in European and international standardisation. Funding may depend on timely delivery and meaningful participation by SMEs, consumers, and environmental and social stakeholders.
he Commission, may finance qualifying European stakeholder organisations representing interests such as SMEs, consumers, and environmental and social groups. Funding supports their participation in European and international standardisation, provision of legal and technical expertise, expert training, contributions to developing and revising standards, and promotion of standards among stakeholders.

Article 16 and Annex III: The Union, through funding administered by the Commission, supports qualifying European organisations that represent SMEs, consumers, and environmental or social interests in standardisation. Eligible organisations must be non-governmental and non-profit, represent the relevant interests at European level, and be mandated by national organisations in at least two-thirds of Member States. Consumer, environmental and social organisations must also be independent of conflicting industry or commercial interests. Funding supports their technical participation, expertise, training, information activities and promotion of European standards.

The regulation follows the the Commission Communication entitled ‘A Digital Agenda for Europe’, should also remain the goal of this Regulation.

The Regulation creates an EU-prescribed but nationally enforced regulatory regime. Unlike the conventional electronic-communications framework, it does not principally depend on national regulators conducting market analysis and imposing obligations on operators with significant market power. Because roaming is inherently cross-border and national regulators could not effectively address excessive roaming charges independently, the EU legislature directly imposes harmonised market-wide obligations.

The goal is to ensure that users of public mobile communications networks, when travelling within the Union, do not pay excessive prices.

It sets out rules enabling the separate sale of regulated roaming services from domestic mobile communications services and the conditions for wholesale access to public mobile communications networks to provide regulated roaming services. The Regulation prescribes the principal substantive rules directly, including wholesale and retail price ceilings, access obligations, transparency requirements, and consumer safeguards. The European Commission supplements these rules through implementing acts, reviews market developments and the Regulation’s effectiveness, publishes information, and may propose further legislative intervention.

National regulatory authorities are the primary operational regulators. Under Article 16, they monitor and supervise compliance, require regulated undertakings to provide information, investigate market developments, intervene on their own initiative, ensure access and interoperability, and order the cessation of infringements. Member States establish and implement penalties.

The Body of European Regulators for Electronic Communications (BEREC) supports coordination rather than independently enforcing the Regulation. It collects and aggregates data from national authorities, develops guidelines and technical guidance, promotes consistent implementation, and advises the Commission.

The Regulation relies primarily on detailed, prescriptive obligations, including direct price controls, access requirements, transparency duties, and consumer safeguards. Providers retain limited discretion over technical implementation, interoperability, and commercial offerings below the prescribed ceilings, but they do not determine the principal regulatory standards or compliance processes.

It is appropriate to provide for a harmonised approach concerning such diligent search in order to ensure a high level of protection of copyright and related rights in the Union. 

The Directive defines orphan works and requires regulated organisations to carry out diligent searches in good faith in respect of each work or other protected subject-matter before using the work or phonogram.

The Directive also address mutual recognition of orphan work status and how to put an end to this status.

Article 6 defined the permitted uses of orphan works, particularly its digitisation.

Directive 2012/28/EU combines EU-level rule-setting with decentralised national implementation. The EU legislature defines orphan-work status, diligent-search requirements, permitted uses, and safeguards. Member States determine the appropriate search sources, designate competent authorities, establish compensation arrangements, and preserve applicable remedies. The Aim of the Regulation as part of a broader Europe 20202 Strategy, is to establish an up-to-date, high-performance infrastructure to help connect and integrate the Union and all its regions, in the transport, telecommunications and energy sectors. The regulation creates a Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) established by this Regulation is to accelerate investment in the field of trans-European networks and to leverage funding from both the public and the private sectors, while increasing legal certainty and respecting the principle of technological neutrality. The estimated investment is around 1 billion Euro.

The regulation points out that telecommunications are increasingly becoming internet-based infrastructures, with broadband networks infrastructure catalysing the use of digital services across a whole range of activities in society.

The Europe 2020 Strategy promotes the Digital Agenda for Europe, establishing a legal framework to boost investment in high-speed internet and related services. The goal is for Europe to have the world's fastest broadband by 2020 using advanced tech. The private sector should play a leading role in rolling out and modernising broadband networks, supported by a competitive and investment-friendly regulatory framework.

Therefore, deploying fast and ultra-fast broadband across the EU, while supporting trans-European digital services, is crucial. Public funding for broadband should avoid market distortions or discouraging investment.

Governance is centered on the European Commission, which programs, selects, funds, monitors, and evaluates telecommunications and digital-infrastructure projects. The Commission selects and supports digital-service infrastructures centrally through grants and procurement. Broadband deployment is promoted through financial instruments managed by entrusted entities and investment vehicles. Member States approve participation, monitor implementation, and certify expenditure, while the Commission retains overall programming, oversight, audit, and evaluation authority.
column17:
The regulation points out that the private sector should play a leading role in rolling out and modernising broadband networks, supported by a competitive and investment-friendly regulatory framework. Where private investment falls short, Member States should undertake the necessary efforts to achieve the targets of the Digital Agenda.

Self-regulation is not operationalised under the Regulation. Private actors participate extensively in financing and implementing broadband and digital-infrastructure projects, but they do not determine regulatory standards or supervise sectoral compliance. Their discretion is financial and operational rather than regulatory.

column16:
The Directive is to contibute to the functioning of the internal market by ensuring that consumers can, on a voluntary basis, submit complaints against traders to independent, impartial, transparent, effective, fast and fair alternative dispute resolution entities. It establishes harmonised quality requirement for ADR entities and procedures to ensure high-quality, transparent, effective and fair out-of-court redress mechanisms.

MS must facilitate access to ADR procedures. MS must ensure that ADR Entities maintain an up-to-date website, providethe parties information, enable to submit complaints offline, enable the exchange of information, and implement the data protection Directive. MS may permit ADR entities to maintain procedural rules allowing them to refuse to deal with a given dispute, for instance for failing to contact the trader, the dispute is frivolous or vexatious. They must provide both sides reasoned explanations when refusing to condier a dispute.

MS must ensure that the people in charge of the ADR possess the necessart expertise ad are independent and impartial. The Directive also places strict rules on how MS states are to guarantee these requirements, including by ensuring they have in place relevant procedures, including having the ability for a collegial body composed of an equal number of representatives of consumer organisations and of representatives of the trader. ADR entities who are empl;oyed or remunerated exclusively by a profesiional organisation of which a trader is a mmber, must have a separate and dedicated budget.

The Directive also describes the exact information and reports that ADR entities must make available on their website. 

The Directive also requires MS to ensure that ADR procedures are effective, implemeting specific requirements, and fair.

MS must ensure that traders inform consumers about the ADR entity by which those traders are covered, when those traders commit to or are obliged to use those entities to resolve disputes with consumers.
They must  also confer responsibility for assisting consumers to the European Consumer Centre Network, on consumer organisations or on any other body. ADR entities and these bodies must make publicly available on their websites and submit to the Commission the list of ADR entities.

ADR entities must cooperate in the resolution of cross-border disputes and conduct regular exchanges of best practices.

Member States designate one or more competent authorities to supervise ADR entities, with a single national contact point where several authorities exist. ADR entities must provide information on their organisation, procedures, independence, performance, and recurring disputes. Competent authorities assess compliance with statutory quality requirements, maintain the national list of approved ADR entities, request corrective action, and remove entities that remain non-compliant. The Commission consolidates and publishes the EU-wide list, while national authorities report every four years on the system’s performance, shortcomings, and possible improvements.
column17: Self-regulation is operationalised through process-based regulation: ADR entities design and administer their own dispute-resolution procedures, subject to binding statutory principles and public oversight. ADR entities retain procedural autonomy and traders may participate through voluntary commitments, but binding statutory standards, public assessment, monitoring and possible delisting substantially constrain that autonomy.
column18: ADR entities are the principal regulatory intermediaries, combining dispute resolution, monitoring and feedback functions. This regulation aims to achieve high level of consumer protection and to contribute to the proper functioning of the internal market by providing an EU online dispute resolution platform between traders and consumers facilitating the independent, impartial, transparent, effective, fast and fair out-of-court resolution of disputes between consumers and traders online.

It builds upon Directive 2013/11. The Commission must develop and operate the ODR platform, including the translation functions necessary for this Regulation, as well as its maintenance, funding, and data security. It must be user-friendly and respect users' privacy. Each MS must designate contact points to provide support to resolution of disputes relating to complaints submitted through the ODR platform. The Commission is also to manage the network of contact points.

The ADR entity which has agreed to deal with a dispute should conclude the ADR procedure within the deadline,
not require the physical presence of the parties or their representatives, and transmit relevant information through the platform, and not be required to conduct the ADR procedure through the ODR platform.

Traders established within the Union that engage in online sales or service contracts, and online marketplaces established within the Union, shall provide an electronic link to the ODR platform on their websites.

ODR contact points are subject to rule of professional secrecy.

The Directive regulates equipment electromagnetic compatibility.
Like the RED, this directive exists in a context in which Directive 1999/5 was amended several times but remains in force for fixed-line terminal equipment, even after the adoption of Regulation 765/2008 and Decision 768/2008.  

MS must ensure equipment on the market complies with this Directive and not hinder its availability due to electromagnetic compatibility issues. They can implement special measures for local electromagnetic problems or safety concerns to protect networks or stations used for safety in specific spectrum situations. They must inform the Commission and other MS about such measures.

MS are responsible for notifying the Commission and other MS of CABs via their notifying authorities, who assess and monitor compliance. They may decide that the notifying authority is their NAB. Notifying authorities must have no conflict of interest with the CAB, operate objectively and impartially, make decisions by competent people different from those conducting assessments. They should not offer or provide conformity assessment or consultancy services on a commercial basis, safeguard confidentiality, and have enough personnel to perform their tasks. 

MS also lay down rules regarding penalties 

Notifying authorities notify the Commission and the other Member States when CABs meet the requirements and provide all documentary evidence. If notification is based on accreditation, then the Commission and MS have two weeks to object; if not, they have two months. These authorities must restrict, suspend or withdraw notification when they ascertain or informed they are no longer meet their obligations, and they must inform the Commission and the other MS. 

The Commission assign notified bodies with the identification number, and it can also investigate and challenge the competence of notified bodies. The MS must provide the Commission with all information relating to the notification or the maintenance of the competence of the notified bodies. If it finds the notified body do not comply they will require the MS to take the necessary corrective measures, including withdrawing the notification. The Commission is also in charge of ensuring that ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between notified bodies through a designated sectoral group.

Same as under RED, the EMC directive relies on Articles 15(3) and 16-29 of regulation 765/2008.

Same as under the RED, National market-surveillance authorities are the principal regulators. They evaluate risky or non-compliant apparatus, require economic operators to take corrective action and may restrict, withdraw or recall products where compliance is not restored. Member States coordinate cross-border measures, while the Commission reviews contested national measures, determines whether EU-wide action is justified and addresses deficiencies in harmonised standards. Notified bodies are informed but do not lead enforcement. The main difference is that the RED additionally contains a specific procedure for formally compliant radio equipment that nevertheless presents a risk.

The Commission coordinates cross-border enforcement, evaluates disputed national measures and decides whether they are justified. It can require EU-wide action, order the withdrawal of unjustified national measures and address deficiencies in harmonised standards, while national authorities remain responsible for direct enforcement. It is assisted by a designated committee

This is a process-based regulation:

Annex I outlines the essential requirements, not the directive. Equipment must ensure electromagnetic disturbances do not interfere with other devices and have immunity against expected disturbances for proper operation. Fixed installations must be installed using good engineering practices, respecting component intended use to meet these requirements.

Regulated entities, especially manufacturers, must ensure their apparatuses meet essential requirements, prepare technical documentation, and conduct conformity assessments. They should then issue an EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE mark, and establish procedures to maintain conformity during ongoing series production. Apparatuses must have identifying elements and include clear user instructions. If an apparatus no longer complies, importers must take corrective action, withdraw it, or recall it. If it poses a risk, authorities should be notified with details of noncompliance. They must also provide authorities with all information and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance. In some situations, importers and distributors are considered manufacturers. 

Conformity assessment follows one of two procedures, through internal production control (Annex II) or EU type examination followed by conformity to type based on internal production control (Annex III). 
Annex II: The manufacturer independently assesses electromagnetic compatibility, prepares technical documentation, controls production, affixes the CE marking and issues the declaration of conformity. No notified body is involved.
Annex III (hybrid): A notified body examines the technical design and documentation, without necessarily examining a specimen, and issues an EU-type examination certificate. The manufacturer then independently ensures that production conforms to the approved type, affixes the CE marking and issues the declaration.

Under Directive 2014/30/EU, conformity assessment bodies must be legally established in a Member State, possess legal personality and operate as independent third parties. They must ensure organisational and personnel impartiality, avoid conflicts of interest and consultancy, maintain technical competence, adequate resources and reproducible procedures, protect confidentiality, carry liability insurance and participate in standardisation and notified-body coordination. They remain fully responsible for subcontracted work, must obtain client agreement and verify and document subcontractor competence. Compliance with relevant harmonised standards creates a presumption that these requirements are satisfied.
These requirements are almost identical to those under the RED, reflecting the common New Legislative Framework template.
They apply for notification, describing the module or modules and the apparatus for which that body claims to be competent, as well as by an accreditation certificate, where one exists.

Notified bodies must also conduct proportionate but rigorous assessments under Annex III. They must require corrective action where non-compliance is found and refuse, restrict, suspend or withdraw certificates when necessary. They must report relevant decisions and changes to the notifying authority, cooperate with market-surveillance authorities, exchange assessment information with other notified bodies and remain subject to national appeal procedures.

The Directive was adopted in the context where Directive 1999/5 was amended several times, but still remains in force regarding fixed-line terminal equipment, as well as, after the adoption of Regulation 765/2008 and Decision 768/2008.  

Its goals are to ensure radio equipment uses the radio spectrum effectively, and the high level of protection of health and safety of persons and of domestic animals. It regulates he making available on the market and putting into service in the Union of radio equipment, which is an electrical or electronic product that intentionally emits and/or receives radio waves for the purpose of radio communication and/or radiodetermination. It exclude specific equiptment listed in Annex I.
MS are to ensure that radio equipment that complies with the Directive can be made available, put into service, and used. They are not to impede the availability on the market in their territory of radio equipment which complies with this Directive.

MS must notify the Commission and other MS of the notifying bodies that can carry out third-party conformity assessment under the Directive. They do so by designating a notifying authority responsible for setting up, carrying out, and monitoring the procedures for assessing and notifying conformity assessment bodies. These authorities may be NABs, but they may also be non-governmental entities. These authorities and bodies must have no conflict of interest, operate with objectivity and impartiality, ensure that decisions regarding CABs are taken by a different person from those who carry out the assessment, and may not offer or provide any activities that conformity assessment bodies perform or consultancy services on a commercial or competitive basis. It must ensure confidentiality. 

MS also lay down the rules regarding penalties and must take all measures to enforce them.

The Commission manages the list of notified bodies based on the notifications it received from the notifying authorities. It may also investigate all cases where it doubts, or doubt is brought to its attention regarding, the competence of a notified body, with the notifying authorities providing it with all relevant information. If it finds non-compliance, it may order the MS to take necessary corrective measures, including the withdrawal of the notification. 
It also provides organisation of exchange of experience between notifying authorities and ensure appropriate coordination and cooperation between bodies notified.

The RED directive directly apply several artciles from regulation 765/2008 regarding market surveillance. National market-surveillance authorities are the principal regulators, inspecting and testing radio equipment and ordering corrective action, withdrawal, recall or market restrictions. Customs and border authorities control equipment entering the EU, while the Commission facilitates information exchange and coordination among Member States. Notified bodies conduct conformity assessment but do not perform general market enforcement.

When Market Surveillance authorities suspect radio equipment poses a health or safety risk, they should evaluate it. If they find non-compliance, they must require corrective action, withdrawal, or recall. If the issue extends beyond one territory, they will notify the Commission and other Member States, providing details on whether non-compliance is due to failure to meet essential requirements or shortcomings in standards. Member States and the Commission can object to national measures, which the Commission may evaluate for compliance with EU legislation. The Commission will inform all parties of its decision. If justified, all Member States must withdraw or recall the equipment; if not, the measure will be recalled.

Article 42 lets Member States require corrective action, withdrawal, or recall even if radio equipment is compliant but poses health or safety risks. MS must promptly inform the Commission and other MS with all details. The Commission then consults with MS and relevant operators, evaluates national measures, and decides their justification. If justified urgency arises to protect health and safety, the Commission can adopt immediately applicable acts.

Article 43 addresses formal non-compliance. It requires MS to order economic operators to correct formal deficiencies concerning CE marking, notified-body identification, declarations, documentation and required information. Persistent non-compliance permits market restriction, prohibition, withdrawal or recall.

The Commission is also in charge of reviewing the Directive.
A designated committee, the Telecommunication Conformity Assessment and Market Surveillance Committee, assists the Commission

This is a process-based regulation:


Article 3: Radio equipment must protect 
Article 3(1): health and safety and an adequate level of electromagnetic compatibility
Article 3(2): ensures effective use and supports the efficient use of radio spectrum in order to avoid harmful interference. 
Article 3(3) - additional regulatory requirements: Radio equipment must meet essential requirements: (a) Interoperates with accessories, especially chargers; (b) Connects with other radios via networks; (c) Can be connected to appropriate interfaces across the Union; (d) Does not harm or misuse networks, avoiding service degradation; (e) Includes safeguards to protect personal data and privacy; (f) Supports features to prevent fraud; (g) Supports features for emergency access; (h) Supports features for users with disabilities; (i) Ensures software can only be loaded if compliance is demonstrated.

Manufacturers must provide the MS and the Commission with information on the compliance of intended combinations of radio equipment and software with the essential requirements. They must carry out conformity assessment.


Regulated entities must ensure their radio equipment complies with the essential requirements, draw up technical documentation, carry out relevant conformity assessments, draw up an EU declaration of conformity, and affix the CE marking. If they consider the radio equipment no longer conforms, they must immediately take the necessary corrective measures, withdraw it, or recall it. If it poses a risk, they must inform the competent national authorities and provide all information and documentation, in paper or electronic form, necessary to demonstrate the radio equipment's conformity with this Directive. 

Similar obligations apply to importers and distributors, who must ensure that the manufacturers have carried out the conformity assessment procedures, and in some situations may be considered the manufacturer themselves.

Self-regulation operates under these obligations. They may benefit from presumed conformity with the essential requirements when they adhere to harmonized standards referenced in the OJEU.

Under Article 17, manufacturers may provide radio equipment in different configurations, but must ensure the conformity assessment confirms compliance for all possible configurations. 

When it comes to compliance of health, safety, and electromagnetic compatibility (Article 3(1)), manufacturers may choose, regardless of whether harmonized standards exist, between internal production control (Annex II), EU-type examination based on internal production control (Annex III), or full quality assurance (Annex IV).

When it comes to spectrum use and additional regulatory requirements (Articles 3(2) and 3(3)), if standards exist, the manufacturer may use internal production controlsl where no standards exist or are partly used, manufacturers must rely on one of the two procedures that require relying on notified bodies:
Annex III: product/type-based third-party assurance followed by internal production control. It combines two modules, B + C: The notified body assesses the product design to verify and attest that the technical design meets the essential requirements, but it does not ordinarily audit the manufacturer’s production system or inspect every manufactured unit. The manufacturer retains responsibility for production conformity. The notified body draws up a report and issue en EU-type examination certificate. It however keep track of acknowledged state of the art, and inform the manufacturer of changes require further investigation

Annex IV: process-based third-party assurance and continuing surveillance. A notified body assesses and approves that quality system and subsequently conducts surveillance, including periodic audits and potentially unannounced visits. Unlike Annex III, the emphasis is not on approving a single product type, but on whether the manufacturer’s organizational processes reliably ensure conformity.

The manufacturer must affix the CE marking and identify the number of the notified body.

Article 26 establishes the eligibility and operational requirements for conformity assessment bodies. They must be legal persons established under Member State law, structurally independent from manufacturers and other interested parties, impartial, professionally competent, adequately staffed and equipped, and protected from commercial or financial pressures and conflicts of interest. They must maintain transparent and reproducible procedures, supervise subsidiaries and subcontractors, carry liability insurance, protect confidential information, and participate in relevant standardization, regulatory and notified-body coordination activities. Business-association bodies may qualify only if their independence and absence of conflicts are demonstrated.

Notified bodies must conduct proportionate but rigorous conformity assessments under Annexes III and IV. When they identify non-compliance, they must require corrective action and, where necessary, refuse, restrict, suspend, or withdraw certificates or quality-system approvals. They must report such decisions and relevant changes to the notifying authority, respond to market-surveillance requests, disclose their activities when requested, and exchange assessment information with other notified bodies. Their decisions must also be subject to an appeal procedure established by the Member State.

CABs may rely on standards referenced in the OJEU to benefit from a presumption of conformity.
When they rely on accreditation, they must wait two weeks before performing their activities, and two months when relying on other assessments. This is the case, unless an objection is raised.

This Regulation replaces Directive 1999/93 (Directive on a Community framework for electronic signatures) and the Commission communication of 26 August 2010 entitled ‘A Digital Agenda for Europe’ identified the fragmentation of the digital market, the lack of interoperability and the rise in cybercrime as major obstacles to the virtuous cycle of the digital economy.

In its conclusions of 4 February 2011 and of 23 October 2011, the European Council invited the Commission to create a digital single market by 2015 to make rapid progress in key areas of the digital economy and to promote a fully integrated digital single market by facilitating the cross-border use of online services, with particular attention to facilitating secure electronic identification and authentication.

The Regulation introduces assurance levels indicating the degree of confidence that an electronic identification means establishes the identity of the person claiming it.

The Regulation aims to ensure an adequate level of security of electronic identification means and trust services. It lays down the conditions for recognising electronic identification means, rules for trust services, and a legal framework for electronic signatures, electronic seals, electronic time stamps, electronic documents, electronic registered delivery services and certificate services for website authentication.

Chapter II establishes a cross-border governance framework for national electronic identification schemes. Member States remain the principal regulators and scheme guarantors, while the Commission standardises and coordinates the cross-border framework. Member States decide whether to notify their electronic identification schemes and remain responsible for the schemes, identification means and authentication procedures under their authority. They must recognise eligible identification means issued under schemes notified by other Member States and cooperate on interoperability, security and peer review. The Commission publishes the notified schemes and adopts implementing acts governing notification, assurance levels, interoperability and cooperation.

Chapter III regulates trust service providers. It establishes the liability of trust service providers for damage caused intentionally or negligently by failure to comply with the Regulation. Trust service providers, rather than Member States, are liable for such damage in accordance with national liability rules. Member States must lay down effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties for infringements.

Each Member State must designate a supervisory body and give it the necessary powers and adequate resources to carry out its tasks. The supervisory body is the principal national regulator. It proactively supervises qualified trust service providers and their qualified services, while acting against non-qualified providers when informed of alleged non-compliance. It reviews conformity assessment reports, conducts or commissions audits, requires corrective action and grants or withdraws qualified status. It also coordinates with other supervisory bodies and data-protection authorities, oversees security breaches and termination arrangements, and reports to the Commission. Supervisory bodies submit annual security-breach summaries to the Commission and ENISA and cooperate in exchanging good practices.

Conformity assessment bodies are the main regulatory intermediaries. They independently audit qualified trust service providers and supply reports that inform supervisory decisions, although the supervisory body retains the authority to grant, maintain or withdraw qualified status.

Member States must also securely maintain and publish machine-readable trusted lists identifying qualified trust service providers and their qualified services. The supervisory body informs the body responsible for the national trusted list of decisions granting or withdrawing qualified status. The national trusted-list body therefore performs an administrative and information function, but does not determine qualified status. The Commission specifies the lists’ technical formats and makes information about the national lists publicly accessible.

Member States also designate public or private bodies to certify qualified signature-creation devices and qualified seal-creation devices and must recognise qualifying signatures and seals in public services. These certification bodies act asassurance intermediaries and are institutionally distinct from conformity assessment bodies. Member States notify the Commission of the certified devices, and the Commission publishes the resulting EU list.

The Commission may refer to standards on the accreditation of conformity assessment bodies and auditing rules under which conformity assessment bodies will assess trust service providers. It also may adopt specifications for the form, presentation, composition, size and design of the EU trust mark for qualified trust services. It may establish a list of standards for the security assessment of information technology products. It also publishes the list of certified qualified electronic signature and seal creation devices.

Self-regulation is operationalised through a prescriptive, process-based regulatory framework.

All trust service providers must implement appropriate measures to manage security risks and keep up with technological developments. They must report security breaches within 24 hours to the supervisory body and relevant authorities. If a breach affects multiple Member States, the supervisory body should notify other concerned authorities and ENISA. 

Qualified trust service providers must be audited by a conformity assessment body every 24 months to confirm that the qualified trust service provider and its qualified trust services fulfill the requirements. The report must be sent to the supervisory authority within 3 days of receiving it. The supervisory authority may audit or request a CAB to perform a conformity assessment of the qualified trust service provider, and must inform the data protection authorities if the assessment indicates a breach of data-protection rules. 

Non-qualified trust service providers can notify the supervisory authority of their intention to offer qualified trust services and submit a conformity assessment report. The authority will verify compliance, and if it concludes they comply, it will grant qualified status and inform the body the trusted lists; any delay beyond three months, must be explained to the provider. Providers may offer the service as qualified only after qualified status has been entered on the trusted list. After qualification, they may use the EU trust mark to identify their qualified trust services in a simple, recognisable and clear manner.

Qualified trust service providers must verify certificate holders’ identities directly or through a third party, using the identification methods specified in Article 24. Equivalent national identification methods require confirmation by a conformity assessment body.

Providers must notify supervisory bodies of changes or termination, employ qualified and reliable staff and subcontractors, maintain adequate financial resources or insurance, disclose service conditions, protect systems and data, prevent forgery and theft, retain relevant records, maintain a termination plan, comply with data-protection law and keep certificate databases updated. They must also publish certificate revocations and provide reliable, automated and free information on certificate validity.

Their administrative and management procedures must correspond to European or international standards. The Commission may identify standards for trustworthy systems and products, compliance with which creates a presumption of conformity with Article 24(2)(e) and (f).

In case of non-compliance with the requirements, the supervisory authority may require corrective action and, after considering the extent, duration and consequences of the failure to meet the requirement, may withdraw the qualified status.

Advanced electronic signatures must be uniquely linked to the signatory, capable of identifying  them, created 
using signature creation data under their sole control, and linked to the signed data so that subsqunent changes are detectable. 

Qualified certificates must meet the requirements laid down in Annex I, while qualified electronic signature creation devices must meet the requirements laid down in Annex II. Annex I prescriptively determines the information that qualified certificates must contain. Annex II sets mandatory technical and procedural safeguards for signature-creation devices and reserves the management of signature-creation data to qualified trust service providers. Private actors retain discretion mainly over the technical means used to achieve these requirements, assisted by voluntary standards that confer a presumption of compliance. Qualified trust service providers implement certificate, validation and preservation processes. However, public authorities retain control through supervision, designation and certification.

Article 32 then prescribes that a validation system must check whether the certificate, device and signature were valid and whether the signed data remains intact. A qualified trust service provider may perform this validation as a regulated service.

Member States may designate public or private bodies to certify qualified electronic signature creation devices and notify the Commission. Certification must be based on a security evaluation following standards for IT security assessment or a comparable process notified to the Commission. The Commission may establish a list of standards for the security assessment of information technology products.

Articles 33–45 extend this regulatory model to qualified validation and preservation services, electronic seals, electronic time stamps, electronic registered delivery services and website-authentication certificates. Qualified trust service providers implement these services within legally prescribed requirements, while retaining discretion over the technical and organisational means used.
